Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In the course of the discussion last evening with respect to the redistribution of 1924 a difference of opinion or rather a difference with respect to certain facts developed between the hon. member at present representing North York (Mr. Lennox) and myself as respects the effect of the addition of the townships of Markham and Vaughan upon the results of the election in 1925. I had made the statement that the addition of the townships of Markham and Vaughan in the redistribution of 1924 gave a distinct advantage to the Conservative candidate. I said later that I was under the impression that the addition of those townships had been subsequently responsible for my defeat in North York. From his seat in this House of Commons last night the hon. member for North York spoke, and his words are reported at page 5288 of Hansard as follows:
If it had not been for the assistance he received-
That is that I received.

from the new municipalities which were added, instead of having a majority of 494 I-
That is, Mr. Lennox.
[DOT]-would have had a majority in the old constituency of 681.
Then later the Prime Minister emphasized what had been said by the hon. member for North York. He is reported at page 5290 of Hansard as follows:
It turns out as a matter of fact that had it not been for the two townships that were added by the redistribution of 1924 he-
That is, myself-
-would have been beaten by a much larger majority than he was.
The facts will be found in the report of the chief electoral officer for the fifteenth general election, 1925, at pages 179 and 180. The figures there given are-

Mr. Chairman, I quite understand the joy of my good friends from Saskatchewan. Redistribution-Mr. Lapointe

Before beginning the
observations I desire to make, which will be very few at this stage of the bill, I wish to refer to a somewhat personal matter. In my absence from the house yesterday I am told that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister seemed to suggest that the special committee that had been formed to negotiate on this question did not sit because I had gone home. I must tell my right hon. friend that I am rather surprised that he is not better acquainted with the facts. The committee, which had made good progress on Friday morning, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) said in the house, was adjourned to 2.30 in the afternoon. I went there at 2.30, so did my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Acadia, but we did not meet the other members. At six o'clock my right hon. friend the member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) told me that we would meet at 8.30. At eight o'clock in the house the Prime Minister suggested that we should proceed with the bill, but on request agreed to postpone it until yesterday. Sir George Perley then crossed the floor and told me that it was useless to go to the meeting room because all was off and there was no possibility of an understanding. I left for home the following morning.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I desire to refer to the two reasons given by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister for the changes which are being made in the electoral map of the province of Quebec. On two occasions he said that first this parliament must undo what had been done in the previous redistribution-[DOT] of course, I assume he means done unfairly. Secondly, he said there must be a readjustment on account of the increase of population in the cities. With these two principles I agree. And I wish to say immediately that in any place or any constituency where any change was made, as my right hon. friend suggests, in 1924, which should not have been made-I go further, any change that was made either fairly or unfairly-I am quite willing to undo. But it is not necessary to change the whole map of the province of Quebec for that purpose.
As to the second reason, the increase of population in the cities, Montreal being given three more seats, it is easy to unite two counties in three places without carving them, without disfiguring them, and provide the additional seats required by the increased population in the city. I repeat; with these two principles I agree, I accept them as a basis for a fair redistribution of seats in the province of Quebec.
Now, Mr. Chairman, before I show what is being proposed, I desire to say, for the benefit of those hon. members who perhaps do not know conditions as they exist in the province of Quebec, how deeply attached the citizens of that province are to their municipal lines, which have existed from time immemorial. That applies to the municipal lines, the county lines, even the district lines. If the province of Quebec has grown united as it has, it is due to that spirit of union which has always existed. Every man, woman and child there in those old parishes of Quebec is as a member of one family. Then, the counties have always existed. There is a moral bond uniting those various places in every constituency of the province of Quebec from time immemorial. It was so in old France, la commune, and even in England. This house is called the House of Commons; the commons representing the counties between which there has always been a noble spirit of emulation and, of competition. The people of Quebec want to live together; they are living together not only municipally, but in their agricultural and other associations. There is a spirit of friendly rivalry between the various counties, the men serve as jurymen in the district courts, and they meet together very often. Now what is proposed is to carve up most of the counties of Quebec, to change absolutely the boundaries and, even to create constituencies by adding together four or five parts of adjoining constituencies. I say it is a desecration of the fair province of Quebec, and I do not believe that this bill will go through in its present form when my right hon. friend has considered the matter as it should be considered. I do not blame him so much as I blame those who know what the conditions are in the province and who yet have not only permitted this thing to be done but have insisted that it should be done.
I propose to show what the situation will be in my owm district of Quebec, where there are twenty-five seats, leaving to my hon. friend the member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) the task of showing what is done in the Montreal district. There are twenty-five constituencies in what is commonly called the Quebec district. Out of those twenty-five it is proposed to keep two and to alter twenty-three. I am going to show, from the first to the last of these twenty-five, whether the principles as set out by my right hon. friend could be applied in the changes which are proposed, namely to undo what has been done or because of the necessity of increasing the number of seats in Montreal. .

Redistribution-Mr. Lapointe
We start with the constituency of Gaspe, which it is proposed to change by the addition of two parishes, being in the townships of Dalibaire and Romieu West, the parishes of Mechins and Capueins. These parishes now are in the county of Matane. For what purpose is this change proposed? Gaspe is one of the largest ridings in Canada in point of territory, as all hon. members know. There are three provincial constituencies included in that area, Gaspe North, Gaspe South and Magdalen Island. To go to Magdalen Island the member for Gaspe has to proceed to Pictou and sail from there. The population of Gaspe at present is 45,617, while Matane has a population of 45,000. Why put those two parishes in Gaspe, where they do not *belong? The constituency of Matane is represented here by a Conservative member, accidentally. Two parishes are being transferred from Matane to Gaspe in the northern part of the riding, but that is not all.
The second constituency is Bonaventure and the Baie des Chaleurs. There again three Liberal parishes are being moved from Matane to Bonaventure in order to try to save the head of my hon. friend from Matane (Mr. Larue). Fie is a nice fellow, but I do not believe it is necessary to disfigure these constituencies and tear away these places which always 'have been in Matane and which should stay there, in order to get rid of some Liberal votes from that constituency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend said they were being put in Bonaventure?

Yes. The first two
parishes to which I refer are being put in Gaspe while the other three are being put in Bonaventure. Matane is changed accordingly. The next constituency is Rimouski, which has a population of 33,151. Three places are being taken from Temiscouata and added to Rimouski, Begon, Ste. Frangoise and Trois-Pistoles. These places are not in the same judicial district as Rimouski; Trois-Pistoles always has been a proud town of Temiscouata county, and it has nothing to do with Rimouski. These places are being taken away from Temiscouata and added to Rimouski in an attempt to deprive my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) of one of his strongholds. Well, I know the conditions there better than they are known by any man in this house, and particularly any man who sat on that committee. I am a native of TemisfMr. Lapointo 1
couata; I was bom a few miles from that town of Trois-Pistoles. I know the feeling of resentment which will be created there if they are forcibly detached from Temiscouata. Trois-Pistoles was the home of Hon. L. P. Pelletier, who was a distinguished Conservative minister from Quebec. He was very fond of his parish, and once he was a candidate in Temiscouata. I should like to know what he would think of the very idea of taking Trois-Pistoles away from Temiscouata in order to serve some political end. Against this I protest, as every one in Temiscouata will protest, and if it is done for the purpose of trying to defeat my hon. friend from Temiscouata let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that he will be elected next time by a much larger majority than he had at the last election.
On the western side of the constituency Notre-Dame-du-Portage, another fine place, is added to the adjoining riding of Kamouraska, which is changed not only by this addition but by the further addition at the western end of three or four parishes from the county of L'lslet. You will see something very interesting here when the maps are laid on the table. They take from the county of L'lslet parishes that usually give a Liberal majority but at the end of the line, near the United States boundary, there is a strong Conservative place, St. Pamphile, which is left in L'lslet. Then L'lslet is added to Montmagny, forming a united constituency of Montmagny-L'lslet. As to this I have nothing to say; I agree that one constituency should disappear there. I submit, however, that L'lslet, with a representation of 19,000 and Montmagny, with 20,000, should be joined without being carved at both ends. This would make a constituency of 39,000, which is still below the unit of representation, and there are many constituencies in the province which have a greater representation. I say L'lslet and Montmagny should be joined as it is proposed, but they should not take away those parts of L'lslet and Montmagny which are Liberal, St. Francois and Berthier, which are perhaps the largest Liberal places in the county of Montmagny. It simply is not fair. Yesterday I was pleased to hear even my hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) say he was prepared to keep St. Francois and Berthier; even he seems to admit that this redistribution is not fair, but he asks why we do not unite Kamouraska and L'lslet

Redistribution-Mr. Lapointe
instead of Montmagny and L'Islet. Well, there is this difference, that Kamouraska already has a representation of 24,000 and with the addition of Notre-Dame-du-Portage that number will be increased, while Montmagny has only 20,000. That is the first reason, and the second is that Montmagny and L'lslet are in the same judicial district. They go together for various purposes, while Kamouraska is in another district altogether. Instead of seeing L'lslet and Montmagny carved in the way they have been, I should prefer to have Kamouraska and L'lslet together. I should prefer to have that rather than see that carving perpetrated. Of course, the natural division is to add L'lslet and Montmagny, for all the rules of the game are in favour of that amalgamation instead of the other one. But I protest against the carving of L'lslet and Montmagny by separating St. Roch des Aulnais, that fine old place in L'lslet, proud of having been part of L'lslet. As my friend from L'lslet (Mr. Fafard) said yesterday, we have the absurdity now that the warden of the county of L'lslet will be an elector of Kamouraska after this has been achieved.
We come now to Bellechasse. My hon. friend, the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) is rather a fortunate being. Bellechasse is what is commonly called a Liberal hive, a strong Liberal constituency. Well, it is being proposed to make it stronger by adding to it part of Dorchester, part of Levis -and you will see how interesting is that part of Levis which goes to Bellechasse-and part of Montmagny.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The population is only
21,000.

Yes, but that is no reason for carving all the Liberal parishes from the adjoining constituency and putting them into Bellechasse.
The next constituency is Levis. Levis is an old historic constituency situated in front of Quebec city. There are two towns. There is the city of Levis, which has a population of about 11,000; there is the town of Lauzon, and there is also the large village of St. Romuald there. It is a county with an historic background. The population as it stands today is 35,656. It is in many respects a city constituency, because the city of Levis is situated in the riding. But it has only a population of 35,656. Now it is proposed by
this bill to take away the old parishes of St. Henri de Levis and St. Jean Chrysostome, which are among the oldest places in the province of Quebec, as well as Riviere Boyer and St. Henri village, and to put them all in the county of Bellechasse, which is situated east of the county of Levis. To achieve this result you have to make a geographical monster. The county of Bellechasse is extended behind the town of Levis and St. Romuald, these fine places being driven from the county of Levis.
But that is not all. The western part of Levis is also composed of Liberal parishes, they are drawn into the county of Lotbiniere, which is another Liberal stronghold, where no Conservative has been elected since confederation. It is simply carrying coals to Newcastle. They have taken from Levis St. Etienne de Lauzon, St. Lambert de Lauzon, St. Nicholas, St. Nicholas Sud and the village of St. Redempteur, and this is being done for the purpose of trying to build up a Conservative seat in Levis. Levis, as I have said, is a city constituency with a population of only 35,000, and it will be reduced to 27,000, when so many rural seats have 40,000, 45,000 and even 50,000 of a population.
This is unfair on the face of it; it is a manipulation that cannot be excused. People laughed when this change was suggested. Nobody believed that it would enter into any sane mind to do this in the county of Levi3, and my hon. friends on the other side representing the province of Quebec know the feelings of the people there. They know for instance that St. Nicholas is the home of the Paquet family as well as of so many other prominent families in Quebec-people who are proud to call themselves sons of Levis. And now they are to be thrown into Lotbiniere.
My hon. friend from Levis (Mr. Fortin) is a good fellow; he is an excellent physician. But let me say to him in all sincerity that I do not think that Levis should be disfigured just to save his political head. I do not think this wound should be inflicted on the fine old constituency of Levis just for the purpose of trying to save a Conservative candidate. Everyone knows that it is not necessary; it is not useful, it is inexcusable. How therefore can we accept such a proposal as this?
Lotbiniere, the next constituency, as I have said, is a Liberal stronghold, and it is being

Redistribution-Mr. Lapointe
added to from Nicolet, from Levis, from Megan tie and from Beauee. My hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Verville) said to me, "There has been an increase on all sides except the north, because in that direction lies the St. Lawrence river and they could not very well put it into Lotbiniere."
Now we come to Dorchester. In Dorchester there is a place called St. Luc, which has be,en erected into a municipality in that county. It has always been there; it was included in Dorchester when it was created a municipality; it has always been part of Dorchester, provincially, federally, municipally and otherwise. It is a small place, but apparently there is virtue in its smallness, because it has always voted unanimously Liberal; it has always given a large Liberal majority. My hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) wishes to put St. Luc in the county of Bellechasse. He mentions also St. Maxime de Scott, which, when originally erected, was situated partly in Beauee and partly in Dorchester. Geographically, as the map will show, it should be in Dorchester, because, as I have said, it is in Dorchester provincially and should be federally as well, as it has been since 1924. I am quite willing to abide by what I say. I think it is a fair thing to put St. Maxime de Scott in Dorchester because it is there provincially and it is there geographically. The population of Beauee is over 50,000 while the population of Dorchester is under 30,000. If my right hon. friend wants to undo what has been done, I am quite willing. St. Maxime de Scott was put there in 1924, so let him take it away if that is the purpose of this redistribution bill.

speechtext: Dorchester forms part of three counties.

Dorchester has existed
since 1850.
Since 1792.

I beg my hon. friend's
pardon.
Since 1791.

Dorchester has always
been an old county by itself and this seems to be a clever distinction made by the hon. member for Dorchester. After all, I think he must have suggested these changes. The municipality of Honfleur is part of the county of Bellechasse but why was it not sent to Bellechasse? It is a Conservative commun-

ity, as is Ste. Sabine, which is partly situated in the county of Bellechasse.

May I ask my hon. friend a question? If he will read the act of 1924 he will see that there was no change made in the bill which is before the house with respect to the municipality of Ste. Sabine. The same thing applies to Honfleur.

The hon. member has not asked a question. He states that no change has been made but these places are Conservative. They are situated partly in Bellechasse but they have been allowed to remain in Dorchester.
Who made the change?

We were compelled to
listen to my hon. friend in the committee and he will have to listen to us now.
That does not say who made the change.

If my hon. friend from Compton will kindly let me proceed, it will be much better. The county of Beauee has been altered to include the parishes which I have mentioned. For the riding of Lot-biniere they took part of the county of Nicolet, but I suppose the hon. member for Richelieu will deal with that matter. In the case of the riding of Megantic, certain Liberal parishes of the county of Wolfe have been thrown in. The voters there have been opposed to the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. LaFleche). As far as the north shore is concerned, I have nothing to say about the three seats in Quebec city. A change has been made in the seat of the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre). A rural section was added in the redistribution of 1914 but I agree that this should be a city seat altogether. I am quite agreeable to the change being made.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: By this change I am losing a normal majority in the rural part of about sixty.

I do not know about
that. My hon. friend might wait to make his remarks a little later.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I wanted to point that out.

I am quite sure my hon. friend is generous enough to give that up. In the case of the riding of Quebec South, the municipality of St. Colombian de Sillery is being taken away, but I have no objection.

Redistribution-Mr. Dupre
This is naturally part of Quebec county to be represented by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion). I have been told that a small addition is to be made in Quebec East. I do not see this in the bill and I will reserve my remarks until later. As far as the constituency of Quebec-Montmor-ency is concerned I do not think the changes will effect any result. But why take away Ste Brigitte de Laval and put it into the county of Charlevoix-Saguenay, which is a province by itself and contains a larger population? I am quite sure when we reach the schedules my hon. friend will give some good reasons for this change. I should like some explanation in connection with Yalcartier. This is part of the county of Portneuf but it has been included in my hon. friend's constituency. Has this change been made because there is an unemployment camp situated there where the men selected by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) are sent? Is it intended that these men shall be in the constituency of Quebec-Montmorency? I do not see any reason why Valcartier which is part of Portneuf should be sent back to Quebec county. There is no population worth mentioning outside of the unemployment camp. The vote in that particular area may not be exactly as my hon. friend desires it to be. The riding of Charlevoix-Saguenay is changed by the addition of Ste Brigitte de Laval. The riding of Portneuf is changed by including Donnacona and some other places which were in Quebec West and by excluding La Tuque. There is a new constituency formed called Lafleche-St. Maurice, which is being made out of Three Rivers, St. Maurice and Champlain. This is very ingenious strategy. The strong Liberal communities of Shawinigan Falls and Grand Mere are being added together in a strong Liberal constituency. The hon. members for Three Rivers-St. Maurice. (Mr. Bourgeois) and Champlain (Mr. Bari-beau) will benefit by being rid of these thorns in their flesh. These are the changes which have been made in the district of Quebec.
If these changes can be justified I am quite willing to listen very attentively to any explanations which may be given. This whole thing is considered as a tremendous gerrymander not only by the Liberal members of the house but by the population as a whole. It is going contrary to elementary political morality. No one in a democracy has the right to lend himself to the loading of the dice in such an obvious and glaring manner. Even newspapers which are usually Conservative have been criticizing this scheme which has been submitted. Even the Montreal Gazette said the other day that they
could not understand why this wholesale change had been made in the province of Quebec. They were curious to know the reason. L'Evenement of Quebec which has alwayH supported this government, had a strong editorial in yesterday's issue protesting against this action. They asked why do this? Why create this embarrassment to the Prime Minister whom we love-
Hear, hear.

I have a great respect
for my right hon. friend, but I am speaking the language of L'Evenement. They are blaming his advisers from Quebec for having done that and they predict that instead of its having the effect which those gentlemen wish to produce, a contrary one will result. This is my initial speech; I have some further remarks to make and if the province of Quebec is sacrificed as is proposed in the bill as submitted, I shall have some frank, honest words to say on the third reading. I think I have given a bird's-eye view of the changes which are proposed to be made in the Quebec district, and I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that you listen to my hon. friend from Richelieu who will give the rest of the story so far as the province of Quebec is concerned.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not been very much associated with the committee on redistribution nor with the committee of elder statesmen which dealt with this question in the last few days. I intend only to answer, to a certain extent, some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). If I may divide his speech into two parts, I may say that he objects on two counts, first, on account of municipal lines, and second, on account of electoral results. I do not know whether I am mistaken, but this is approximately the division I can make of my hon. friend's speech.
Of course when changes occur, they cannot be made unless somebody on either side of politics is hurt to a certain degree; but speaking generally, and thereby answering my hon. friend by a sweeping statement, I may say that the federal distribution has nothing to do with municipal lines. Provincial constituencies are not changed; we do not and we cannot touch them and it is on provincial demarcations that the county councils and judicial districts are based. Therefore all the arguments of my hon. friend about tampering with constituencies and the harm that can be done to every one of them, municipally or provincially, by the changes he describes, falls to the ground.
Redistribution-Mr. Dupre
Why not put St. Sauveur into Temiscouata?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
May I point out again to
my hon. friend, since I think there are eighty-two provincial ridings-
Ninety.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Thank you-ninety provincial ridings and only sixty-five federal constituencies, necessarily the demarcations and lines of the provincial constituencies have to be changed; we cannot do otherwise.
But there is another aspect and it is to consider the changes in a general way. I deplore the fact that in the district of Quebec we had to lose one constituency on account of the adjustment based on urban population.
May I ask my hon. friend a question?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

He says that the changes
in Quebec were made on account of the increase in urban population. Is that the reason that the new rural constituencies Ghapleau and Lafleche-St. Maurice have been created?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
seem to understand my point. I am telling him that one of the main reasons there were some changes and new lines of demarcation necessary in the district of Quebec was that we had to lose one constituency which necessitated new lines in some others.
If my hon. friend permits me, I do not wish to interrupt him again-
Sit down!

The Solicitor General is
more courteous than is the hon. member for West Essex; he allows me to put a question. My hon. friend should learn manners from the Solicitor General; it will improve the tone of the house.
Will the hon. gentleman ask his question?

Yes. We have been told that changes have been made in the rural seats because of the three new seats in Montreal. I ask the Solicitor General why it has been decided by the government to create two new rural seats, one in the Ottawa and the other in Three Rivers district. If three new seats in Montreal were too many, why did the government decide to create two new rural seats when there was no necessity for so doing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will follow me, he will understand my point. I will answer him immediately. Since we had to find new lines in Quebec district and lose one constituency in the district of Three Rivers and one in the district of Montreal, necessarily we had to form new divisions and in some special cases we had to create new constituencies. I deplore, as I said, that we had, on account of the readjustment of urban population, to lose one seat in the district of Quebec. If I could have prevented	this, I would have	done so
with great pleasure, and in fact I tried but I did not succeed. At one time there was a question of taking away two constituencies from the district of Quebec and to this I objected. Yesterday I heard the hon. member for L'lslet (Mr. Fafard) complaining about the new lines in his constituency. I agree with him that this is most unfortunate, but we could not help it. I agree also that the hon. member for L'lslet, who has always been an acquisition to this house and who is a distinguished member, will find a way to come back, because we like his presence here.
I think he will.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
But if hon. members will consider the new districts, they will see how everything has been divided. For instance, around Quebec there are on the south shore from Levis up to Kamouraska different constituencies side by side. What is the result of the new adjustment? There is Levis with a population of 28,548; Dorchester next to it with a population of 27,156; Montmagny-LTslet, the ne<w proposed1 constituency, with a population of 30,869, and Bellechasse with a new population of 27,480, and Kamouraska with 30,852. Thus there are five constituencies side by side, each with approximately the same population.
My hon. friend has been talking about Levis. May I point out to him that with the new adjustment Levis will have about the same population as the four constituencies around it. Besides that, under the new adjustment there are nine constituencies in the province of Quebec with populations less than the population of Levis. Taking first Levis, with a population of 28,548, the others are:
Population
Argenteuil	 27,885
Bellechasse	 27,480
Chapleau	 21,705
Chateauguay-Huntingdon	 24,412
Dorchester	 27,156
Shefford	 28,262
Stanstead	 25,118
Vaudreuil-Soulanges	 21,154
Wright	 27,107

Redistribution-Mr. Dupre
Therefore we have nine constituencies with populations less than the population of Levis. Of these constituencies with populations less than Levis there is one new one, five constituencies represented by Conservative members and three represented by Liberal members.
If, being dissatisfied you put back into Levis the parishes of St. Henri and St. Jean, you will have the following result: The population of Belleehasse will drop down to 24,315 and the population of Levis will increase to 31,713. But as it is, with the new proposals the populations of Levis and Belleehasse will be approximately the same.
If my hon. friend from Quebec East will revert to Quebec South, which is an urban constituency in the heart of the city of Quebec, he will see that Levis which is not fully urban, but only semi-urban, has with the new adjustment a population of 28,548 while Quebec South, which is fully urban, will have a population of 33,441, which is only 4,893 more than Levis. I have heard that in the past the county of Richelieu which could be compared to a certain extent to the county of Levis, because both contain a city of about 11,000 population-has remained for twenty-one years with a population of approximately 21,500. I shall not dare to add that very likely the stationary character of its population was due to the fact that it was a Liberal constituency. I should not like to be accused of such an argument, but the fact is that Levis has 28,500 while Richelieu, for 21 years, has remained at the figure of 21,500. Another reason for the change in Levis is that Belleehasse, next to Levis, has a population which does not increase or decrease. In fact in the last ten years the population of Belleehasse has decreased by about 106. It is stationary. If the hon. member for Quebec East will refer to the statistics he will find that the population of Levis increases from 3,000 to 4,000 every ten years. If this increase continues in ten years Belleehasse will have the same population as it has now, while the population of Levis will be about 32,000 or 33,000, which is approximately the same as that of Quebec South at the present time.
A moment ago I heard the hon. member for Quebec East deploring the fact that the Paquet family of Levis will for federal purposes have to live in the county of Lotbi-niere. I may add that this is a most respectable old family. They are countrymen, farmers, and real gentlemen. It is a family for which I have as much respect as my hon. friend. They have given some remarkable men to politics, to the professions, to agriculture and to industry. I hope however that my hon. friend does not mean to say that the fact that the Paquet family has been thrown into Lotbiniere for federal purposes is a disgrace to them. The county of Lotbiniere, so far as I can see, is as good a county as Levis or Belleehasse. The Paquet family for federal purposes will belong to the county of Lotbiniere, and for provincial purposes will continue to belong to the county of Levis.
Coming back to Dorchester, I have a few words to say. I think the hon. member for Dorchester is able to take care of himself.
I have not to defend what has taken place; in fact, I do not know what has taken place, because I was a member of no committee and attended no sessions of redistribution committees. I say to my hon. friend from Quebec East, however, that very likely we can agree on Dorchester for the following reasons: My hon. friend from Quebec East admits that so far as the parish of Ste Max-ime de Scott is concerned, he has really no serious objection, because it is a parish which belonged to the county of Beauce (Mr. Lacroix). So far as the two parishes of St. Zacharie and St. Aurelie are concerned-
They are not in the bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, because there has been a misprint. I understand there will be an amendment, because the county of Dorchester has not been properly described in the bill before us.
Then I shall have to oppose that. It is still worse.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The proposal is to add the parishes of St. Zacharie and St. Aurelie to the county of Beauce. I might say that this has been done with the approval of the hon. member for Beauce. I have his own figures and his own writing before me.
That has nothing to do with it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Let us study the situation in the district of Quebec, as outlined by my hon. friend. What is the result of these changes? I am considering what might happen from an electoral point-of-view, and I am assuming for the sake of argument that the figures will be the same as in 1930. What is the result? Quebec East, which has been so well represented by the ex-Minister of Justice, remains as it is. Therefore chances are that he would be elected by the same majority.
More.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Quebec South is about the same. The Liberal majority by the new changes, as far as Quebec South is concerned, is just a little increased.
Redistribution-Mr. Dupre

As far as I am concerned, Quebec West is about the same, with the difference that by taking away the rural part of my constituency I will lose 60 votes of the Conservative majority. In Lotbiniere, basing ourselves always on the same figures, the Liberal majority will be increased; I am sure my hon. friend from Quebec East will not object to that. In Bellechasse, always taking the same figures, the Liberal majority will be increased. In Charlevoix-Saguenay it will be about the same, perhaps the Liberal majority may be increased by a few votes. Is that anything to complain about? In Kamouraska the majority will be increased also; what have my friends opposite to complain about? In Bonaventure the Liberal majority will be increased. In Gaspe the Liberal majority will be increased. My hon. friends smile as I give these figures-
Because you seem to be a real fortune-teller.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am only basing myself on the figures of the last election. In Portneuf there is a change, both parties will be about equal. I hope my friends will not complain at having to fight in a constituency where the chances are equal. InMontmagny and in Que-bec-Montmorency it will be about the same as in 1930. In Dorchester and Levis I admit that the Conservative majority might be increased and that, based on the figures of 1930 the chances of the Conservative candidate will be better.
Listen to that!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If you are kind enough to follow my argument-
This is not an argument, it is a prognostication!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-there are seven or eight constituencies where the Liberal chances will be increased, and only two where the Conservative chances will be increased. Is that unfair to my hon. friends?
There are other arguments, which I will not cover just now because they will be discussed later in connection with the different constituencies. But there is one thing to which I wish to draw attention. It is this: my hon. friend from Quebec East has spoken about the general principle of municipal lines, judicial districts and so forth. My answer, and I ask pardon for repeating it, is that the federal demarcations have nothing to do with the municipal lines or judicial districts, because these municipal lines and judicial districts are based on the provincial constitu-

encies, which are not changed, and which we cannot change. But there is another principle much more important than that. It is that in the new redistribution there will be in the province of Quebec no more solid blocs. There will be no more Conservative and no more Liberal blocs. I draw to the attention of my hon. friend from Quebec East the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier many years ago when he said it would be a most unfortunate situation if we had a Conservative or a Liberal bloc either in Ontario or Quebec.
Did the Liberal bloc elect twenty-seven Conservatives in the last election?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That does not change my argument; my hon. friend does not seem to understand me. He is going back now to the old divisions.. We must be fair, we must be broadminded and we must think of principles and ideals. I say it is a most unfortunate situation when there is in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario a solid bloc either. Liberal or Conservative. And I draw the attention of my hon. friends opposite to this fact, that we have been able to fight and we have been able to win some seats when we were in the opposition, and we are going to fight again and to maintain our position in the next federal election. What I want them to understand is that the days of Liberal domination are finished.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.
That is a good explanation.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that the last word uttered by the hon. Solicitor General will be regretted by him when he becomes a little more calm. His last observation is far from indicating a spirit of fairness on the part of the government in the working out of the redistribution project that is being placed before the house at the present time.
I quite realize the difficulties encountered when preparing a redistribution of the province of Quebec. Under the British North America Act we are in a very difficult and embarrassing 'position; we: cannot increase the number of seats beyond the sixty-five allotted to us by the pact of confederation, and we have to take care of the English minorities in that province. I may say to the honour of the citizens of Quebec that that obligation has been more than respected during the past years. So when it comes to figuring out the allotment of constituencies in

Redistribution-Mr. Cardin
Quebec we are limited by those two important considerations. And it is impossible to attain a satisfactory result when drafting the boundaries of constituencies in the province of Quebec if too much weight is given to the factor of population. It is utterly impossible to equalize population in the constituencies of that province in view of the two considerations I have just indicated. Then there is also the big city of Montreal, and the city of Quebec which is growing very rapidly; it is impossible, I repeat, to have equality of population in all the constituencies of that province. Since confederation there has been always a big discrepancy between the population of certain constituencies, even in the rural sections of the province. So I am driven to the conclusion, and I take the risk of expressing what is in my mind that the time has come or will be here very soon when the basis of dividing seats for the federal house will have to be changed and the British North America Act amended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

It is unfair, with the growing population of the province of Quebec to keep our representation at the same number, 65 seats, when we have to take care of the English-speaking minorities as we have been doing in the past years. I am not afraid of a change in the British North America Act in that respect. When our number was fixed at 65 at the time of confederation it was done in order to protect the populations in the small provinces of Canada. But the trend of population has not been as foreseen by the fathers of Confederation; their estimates have proven wrong. At the time of confederation the maritime provinces were afraid, not of the province of Quebec, but of the province of Ontario, which at that time was expected to develop more rapidly than any other and to increase its population much more than Quebec. They wanted to be protected against the increase of the province of Ontario by assurance against reduction of seats in certain cases. The exception which was made at the time was for the protection of the maritime provinces, but circumstances have been such that the province of Ontario in fact is benefiting by the exception which was made with the intention of helping the maritimes. So the principle must be redrafted, and the sooner it is done the better it will be, and the sooner we will have a fairer representation in the House of Commons.
If I understood his words correctly the Prime Minister said that his party had made some sacrifices in New Brunswick and Nova
Scotia in order to avoid altering the boundaries of constituencies. I believe the Prime Minister said that in one province the Conservative party lost one seat because they wanted to respect the boundaries of the constituencies. Let me tell the right hon. gentleman in all frankness that if he would apply the same principle to the province of Quebec this question of redistribution would be settled in no time at all. It would be the easiest thing in the world to deal with this matter if the right hon. gentleman would apply that principle to the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If I may interrupt the
hon. gentleman, I trust he realizes that the electoral divisions in Quebec now comprise parts of many communities. For instance, the old county of Dorchester takes in parts of three provincial counties. That is the point I was trying to make.

Yes, but I may answer that this situation prevails in a relatively small number of the constituencies in Quebec. It applies very little in the Montreal district, which has from forty to forty-two seats. I am quite ready to agree that this principle of respecting boundaries could not be applied everywhere; I admit that in certain cases exceptions should be made, but I urge upon the Prime Minister that generally speaking the principle he has applied in making sacrifices in the maritime provinces should be applied in the province of Quebec as well. I still hope, as I have said to a number of my hon. friends who are complaining with regard to the redistribution bill, that when the true picture is placed before the Prime Minister he will set aside some of the recommendations which have been made by his supporters and insist on having a measure brought before the house which will be fairer and more equitable to all parties in Quebec. I still have the firm belief that before we are through with the schedules many changes will be made which will bring about a better understanding among the citizens of the province of Quebec and will indicate more broadmindedness on the part of those who have the majority in this house. It is all very well to speak of equalizing the population, but if this is the aim why reduce the representation in counties which at present are below that unit; why reduce them still more? There are several constituencies in Quebec below the unit of representation, according to the last census. Instead of trying to increase them or even keeping them as they are and as they have been for many years, it is now proposed to reduce their population.
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

Then a new constituency is to be created in the northern section of Quebec, in order to give a chance to a very nice gentleman, the hon. member for Three Rivers-St. Maurice (Mr. Bourgeois), and in order to give a chance to another very nice and bright young man, the hon.. member for Champlain (Mr. Bari-beau). These hon. members are to be helped by taking from their constituencies a certain number of Liberal centres. A new county is created, with a population of only 21,000. This is the answer to the argument of my good friend the Solicitor General that so far as possible we must equalize the population in Montmagny and L'lslet and the two adjoining counties.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Would my hon. friend allow me a question? Would he tell me the area of that new constituency?

The area does not mean
anything when there is no one living in that area. You could take all the northern section of Quebec or all Ungava and you would not have a large population.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question.

It is an answer; there is a small population in that territory at the present time. The only justification for the assertion of the Minister of Marine is that in the future that area may be developed. Many things may happen in the future in these constituencies in the centre of Quebec which are being carved up to-day. By these proposals constituencies with populations of 40,000, 42.000 and 45,000 will be increased to 50,000, 55,000 and possibly 60,000 in the next ten years; so we had better bank on realities rather than expectations, as my good friend the Minister of Marine is trying to do in order to justify the present project. There is no justification for reducing the representation in counties which are too small now, or for creating a smaller constituency in a new section, in order to protect two members already sitting in' this house. I wonder why hon. gentlemen opposite, representing constituencies where they have been elected by majorities of 500, 600, 1,100 and so on, are afraid to go back to the electors a second time. I cannot understand that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me a question? I do not want to interrupt his argument, but the same point would apply to the Liberal party, because I have already named seven or eight constituencies in which the Liberal majorities will be greatly increased. fMr. Cardin.]

Yes, I can see the position taken by the Solicitor General. He is trying to hive all the Liberals he can gather together in a certain section of the province in order to weaken the chances of the Liberals in the section where the Conservatives were elected at the last election. That is the whole story, the whole purpose of the present redistribution bill, and I say hon. gentlemen opposite lack a certain amount of courage if they are afraid to go back to the electors who sent them here, if they are afraid to face them under the same conditions that existed during the election of 1930. My hon. friend the Solicitor General said that he was very strongly opposed to the changing of provincial counties, and that this bill does not change them. Let me tell him that in the proposed redistribution of the Montreal seats and the rural section of the district of Montreal the boundaries of the provincial seats are being changed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We cannot change the provincial districts.
It is being done.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, we cannot touch the judicial lines because they are based on the provincial constituencies. My theory is that whatever changes may be made in federal constituencies the provincial constituencies and judicial lines remain the same.
But the provincial constituencies do not remain the same under this bill; the provincial constituencies are changed, and I can give a very good illustration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have no authority to change provincial lines.

That is not the point; we are not discussing here any changes in the judicial districts of the province of Quebec. We are talking about provincial districts, provincial constituencies and federal constituencies. If I gathered rightly the observations of the Solicitor General, he said that the provincial counties were not being changed by this redistribution. Perhaps I was wrong in my interpretation of his remarks, but I think that was what he said. Well, my answer to the hon. gentleman is this: You are changing the boundaries of the provincial counties; you are changing them in the district of Montreal, and changing them very materially.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We are not following the lines of the provincial counties.

Redistribution-Mr. Cardin
I thank the Prime Minister. I say, you are not following the lines of the provincial counties in Quebec.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We agree on that.

The Solicitor General said also that we have to make changes because the Quebec district has to provide one seat to be given to Montreal, or to the northern section of the province of Quebec. If the Quebec district has to provide one rural seat to be given to Montreal or to the north, why change all the other constituencies in the Quebec district? What has Levis to do with the counties of Montmagny and L'lslet, which are supposed to be joined in one way or another? To obtain that additional county for the Quebec district it would be sufficient to join two counties or possibly four. But what about the rest? Is the division of the county of Levis changed for the purpose of giving one seat to Montreal? Is the county of Gaspe changed in its limits for the purpose of giving one seat to the north? They are mere changes of parishes here and there. You are not taking the seat you want for Montreal from the changes which are being made in most of the constituencies in the Quebec district.
Neither in Temiseouata.

My hon. friend referred kindly to the county of Richelieu, which had been kept for a considerable time a small county of 21,000. For his information I may say that the county of Richelieu has been changed. It was changed in 1892. The parish of St. Marcel of the county of Richelieu was placed in the county of Bagot. That parish came back later on to the county of Richelieu, and in 1914 when the redistribution was carried out by the government then in power, the parish of St. Marcel was placed in the county of Yamaska. Changes have been made, though, I am ready to admit, not of very great importance. But the county of Richelieu is not the only county with a small population and which has not changed. There are much smaller constituencies in Canada and in the province of Quebec than the county of Richelieu; and I do not object very much to the increase which the present redistribution bill makes in Richelieu. They are giving the constituency now, according to this redistribution, part of Yamaska, part of Yercheres and part of St. Hyacinthe, and they are increasing the population to 35,000. It is more 38,000 than 35,000. I do not object so much on that account, because I realize that my constituency, although it was not the smallest,
should be increased; I admit that. But they are making changes for which there is no justification at all.
If I understood rightly the main argument of the Solicitor General, the justification was that they increased the chances of the Liberals in the constituencies they have, and increased the chances of the Conservatives in their constituencies. That is the principle of the whole redistribution which has been forced upon the Prime Minister of the country and which I am sure he will not accept when he is in possession of all the facts which are going to be placed before him.
I am not going to dwell very long on the situation in the island of Montreal. I confess that, living in a rural section of the province of Quebec, I am not as familiar with the island of Montreal as are the residents of that city. But the island of Montreal was practically settled when the committee of elder statesmen met, and when I was called before that committee as a witness; I got the impression that the island of Montreal had been agreed to. If that understanding had been signed at that time there would be no difficulty in regard to the island of Montreal. The difficulty came when the elder statesmen of the Conservative party consulted with their supporters in the island of Montreal and surrounding districts. The elder statesmen were quite ready to accept the plan as it had been modified, but the other gentlemen who advised those statesmen wanted to put forward a project of their own and so forced a disagreement on the committee.
I cannot understand for the life of me why, according to the redistribution bill which is before us, the county of St. Mary in the island of Montreal should disappear-the county which is more clearly defined than any other; the county which is more explicitly described on the map; the county which is most perfect geographically speaking, so far as the city of Montreal is concerned, and a county which has a population of 66,000. I cannot see why that population of working men, labouring people who have been together for twenty or thirty years, knowing clearly the boundaries of their constituency, and with a population of 66,000-I cannot understand, I say, why that county should disappear and why a new county is created with a population which is smaller than the population of St. Mary. St. Mary disappears, and they are creating a new county which is called Lafontaine. That county of Lafontaine, according to the figures given to us, is going to have a population of only 65,000 while the county of St. Mary, which is to disappear, has a population of 66,000, and is moreover more easily described and is much
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

more interesting from the point of view of geography and regularity of lines.
What is the reason? Why do away with St. Mary and create another constituency? The county of St. Mary could have been increased a little, as all other constituencies in the county of Montreal have been increased. The county of Hochelaga could have been increased also, and St. Mary could have been left where it is at present, and no one would have suffered on that account. But why make a gerrymander of this sort in the heart of the island of Montreal in order to create a new constituency, doing away with an old one against which nothing can be said? I repeat, I cannot understand why that county of St. Mary is to disappear.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not aware, was he not told by the members of the committee, that our friends on our side agreed to restore the division he is mentioning, St. Mary-
Yes, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -not because we thought it was a better redistribution but because we wanted to yield to the wishes of the hon. gentleman's friends. Is he not aware of that? Is it his wish now, is it the wish of my hon. friends opposite, to make political capital? If it is we will again yield to their wishes if they desire to make political capital out of it.

No political capital is being made. The only political capital which is being sought is sought by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine, as I will show in a moment. When there was a meeting before the elder statesmen the question was discussed with respect to the county of St. Mary. The only difficulty was that St. Mary was disappearing. The members from Montreal were asked for suggestions and they suggested that a new constituency to be called Lafon-taine should not be created but that the populations of St. Mary and the other adjoining constituencies should be increased. But what were the observations of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley)? He said: In doing that are you not destroying what has been practically agreed upon in the other sections of Montreal? The answer was, 'no." This would only affect St. Mary, St. James and Hochelaga. The hon. member for Argenteuil did not want to destroy St. Mary or change the boundaries of St. Antoine and other constituencies in Montreal. He said that they might agree to effect changes in regard to St. Mary without changing what 
had been practically settled upon and accepted by certain Conservative members from the island of Montreal. He was told that that would not change the position and he said that they might agree. What is the new proposal now being made? It is that a change be made with regard to Outremont. Other changes were to be made an other sections of the island of Montreal. That is the proposal to which the Minister of Marine referred. If he would come to us with the proposal which was practically accepted by the hon. member for Argenteuil and accepted to a large extent by himself, there would be no objection on the part of Montreal. Why is there any objection? It is because they want to do something new and make changes on the island of Montreal which would be contrary to the views expressed by the hon. member for Argenteuil. That is why we cannot accept the new proposal which has been made. It is not the proposal to which the Minister of Marine agreed before the committee of elder statesmen. If it was, I would be the first one to advise my colleagues from the island of Montreal to accept.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The suggestion made with regard to Outremont was to restore that seat. The objection raised by the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) was that we were changing the lines of Outremont, and we are now suggesting that they be restored.

Why go back on the proposals which were made three or four weeks ago after it was practically agreed in the special committee that St. Mary should be restored without disturbing the other constituencies except by increasing the populations of the surrounding constituencies? Why revive old difficulties? That is what my hon. friend is trying to do at the present time.
I hope I shall be pardoned for the heat of my observations. I have no desire to hurt the feelings of anyone but I have not the advantage of being able to switch to soft tones. It is my nature and I cannot change it. I do not mean any offence to hon. gentlemen who do not share my views. There may be much heat but there is no ill feeling at the bottom of my heart.
Let us leave the island of Montreal and go to the constituency of Ohateauguay-Huntingdon. To a large extent the county of Huntingdon is to remain in the same position as it was. It is a small county which has been represented practically continuously by an English speaking representative. As

Redistribution-Mr. Cardin
far as I am concerned I am willing to make sacrifices in order that this riding shall not be disturbed. This is a small constituency but it is being reduced still further by this proposal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It will have 4,000 more
than Richelieu.
The present proposal reduces it by over a thousand. If it will satisfy the Prime Minister, I will not object to leaving it as it is. I would be ready to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It was done to meet
our hon. friends' wishes, as a matter of fact.

I beg your pardon, it was
not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: You objected to joining Beauharnois and Soulanges.

I objected to joining two counties which were separated by lake St. Erancis and the St. Lawrence river without any bridge communication. That was the proposal made by the Minister of Marine. There is not even a regular ferry service and in the winter time it is impossible to go across. The only justification which could be offered by my hon. friend was that some day there might be a bridge. I know they will say that they did not change Soulanges which has only 21,000 population. I asked them to change it logically by taking in Ste. Anne de Bellevue which at the present time is in Jacques Cartier. That would be the natural way to increase the population of Vaudreuil-Soulanges. It cannot be increased to the north because of the lake of Two Mountains; it cannot be increased to the south because of lake St. Francis and the St. Lawrence, but it could be increased by taking in Ste. Anne de Bellevue. There are two bridges crossing the Ottawa river to provide communication. But Yaudreuil-Soulanges remains as it is because they do not want to increase it in the logical and fair way. That is why it is being kept at 21,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
You would have to
cross two rivers.
Where there are two highway bridges.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Toll bridges.
That is better than trying to cross the St. Lawrence and lake St. Francis where there are no bridges.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There is a railway
bridge.

I have no great authority
to speak for my party but as far as I am concerned personally I would be willing to accept Chateauguay-Huntingdon as it is at the present time. The proposal is to take Laoolle in St. John's-Iberville and join it to Chateauguay-Huntingdon. I cannot see any justification for that and I would be inclined to oppose this transfer. But that is not my main objection to what is proposed for Chateauguay-Huntingdon. My hon. friend will understand me when I say that in the county of Huntingdon there is a parish called Ste. Barbe. The proposal of the bill is to take that parish of Ste. Barbe from the county of Huntingdon and transfer it to the county of Beauharnois which is going to be a hive to which surrounding Liberals will be brought. That is not all. There is in the county of Beauharnois the little Conservative parish of St. Etienne. It is taken from the county of Beauharnois down to the county of Huntingdon to assist the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Moore). That is the present proposal which is being made and it is the one to which I very seriously object. It is not a matter of joining counties together or adjusting population or increasing population. My hon. friend by that process is reducing the population of his constituency, carving the parish of Ste. Barbe from it and taking in its place the parish of St. Etienne. The reason is obvious; it is to get rid of the little parish of Ste. Barbe which is Liberal and to take in the parish of St. Etienne which is Conservative and which he wants to get nearer to his heart. That is the position. As regards the constituency of Chateauguay-Huntingdon, if that is not gerrymandering, I wonder what gerrymandering is. In reality is it worth while to change the configuration of the county of Beauharnois, to make a hole in the southeastern boundary of that county in order to get the small parish of St. Etienne?
Not a hole.

Yes, it is a hole and as
far as the municipality of Ste. Barbe is concerned, it is a little block which is added to the extreme southwestern end of the county of Beauharnois. These changes cannot be justified by any process of imagination nor for any reasons which can be advanced. If we are to apply the principle advanced by the Solicitor General that we have to find constituencies to give to Montreal and other places, it is not necessary to change Ste. Barbe or St. Etienne for that purpose; there is no reason for doing so. But I repeat, I would be ready, so far as I am concerned,

Redistribution-.1/r. Cardin

to leave my hon. friend's constituency the way it is at present.
As regards the new proposal which is being made, in view of the fact that my constituency has been compared by the Prime Minister with that of Chateauguay-Hunting-don, under the new redistribution, I can say that the constituency of the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon will have a population of 24,000 and the new constituency of Richelieu will have a population of 35,000, so if there has been any discrepancy in the past the present bill takes care of it so far as I am concerned, but not so far as the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon is concerned.
Let us make a trip into the adjoining county of Beauharnois which is Liberal. The county of Beauharnois which they wanted to send across the St. Lawrence or across lake St. Francis, they wish to add to the county of Laprairie which is also Liberal. But unfortunately there is no contact between the two.
The obstacle!

Yes. They are separated by a portion of the county of Chateauguay and the present bill is creating a corridor in order to join the counties of Beauharnois and La-prairie. Inspired by what was done by the diplomats of Europe after the war, my hon. friends have created a new corridor; they have transplanted on the soil of Quebec the idea which originated in the minds of European diplomats. So we have a corridor joining the counties of Beauharnois and Laprairie. At a certain section it is veiy narrow. If I were to carve on a sheet of paper the counties of Laprairie and Beauharnois and try to keep them together by the small piece of paper which would represent the corridor, it would not keep them together; it could not stand the 6train; it is so flimsy that on account of the divisions of the parishes which exist there, you could not join the two counties properly. Even at that, if there was a necessity of uniting constituencies, it is a lesser evil to have Laprairie and Beauharnois that way than to have Beauharnois and Vaudreuil-Soulanges on the other side of lake St. Francis. If that had to be done to help those constituencies to disappear and to give one more seat to the island of Montreal, arguments could be put forward and settlements reached. But I repeat what I said in regard to Chateauguay-Huntingdon: If Beauharnois is joined to Laprairie through that corridor, it should be joined as a whole, not after having the parish of St. Etienne carved out of it and the small parish of Ste. Barbe added to it. If you want (Mr. Cardin.]
to join those two constituencies, join them as they are through the corridor narrow as it is. If this were the only objection, I would not fight very strenuously in order to come to an agreement and do away with the unpleasant example which is at present being given to the country. I cannot think-and I am most sincere in saying this-that in these dying days of the session, in these days when we are ready to go home and when a large number of members have already left, in the end we are going to be forced to swallow the proposal which has been made and we shall not be able to come to some understanding. Surely there should be a possibility, with every one of us making a little compromise, of reaching an agreement and settling the matter amicably as has always been done in the past. The Prime Minister, when speaking the other day, said that on another occasion he was on a committee and they did not agree at first; they fought strongly, one against the other; they had conflicting proposals, but the fact remains that in the end they agreed. After a strenuous fight, they came to an understanding. Why not try to come to an agreement in this case? Why not be as generous as we can, make little concessions here and there and do away with the follies in connection with certain sections of Quebec which are proposed by this bill? Why not do away with that and try to agree on general lines? If we follow generally the principle advocated by the Prime Minister and try to preserve as far as possible the county boundaries, we can reach an agreement and the small difficulties outside can be very easily adjusted by the leaders of the two parties.
At one o clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to the question asked yesterday by the right hon. the leader of the opposition, I have to inform him that section 17 of the British North America Act, 1867, provides that there shall be one parliament of Canada, consisting of the Queen (King), an upper house, styled the Senate, and the House of Commons, and it is the considered view of His Majesty's government in Canada that a resolution passed by one house of parliament is legally effective only as an expression of the opinion of those who support such resolution in that house, and this is particularly true with respect to the prerogatives of the crown.
The sovereign can only be deprived of a prerogative right by statute of parliament, in very special form, which the government does not propose to introduce. There is apparently no opportunity at this time for discussion of the matters referred to by the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house again in committee on Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons-Right Hon. R. B. Bennett-[DOT] Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
53719-336J

When the committee rose at one o'clock I was dealing with the proposed arrangement between the counties of Beau-harnois and Laprairie. Before proceeding any farther I should like to insist upon the point which has been disputed-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken forty minutes, and should not speak again before another member has spoken.

Mr. Chairman, last night when the committee rose I was saying that the reason we objected to the division of Montmagny and L'Islet was .that it took away the Liberal majority. The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet suggested that-
Mr. LaVERGNE: Not yet.

The hon. member for Montmagny suggested, as a counter proposition, that L'Islet should be put with Kamouraska. I was about to answer him upon that point when-
Mr. LaVERGNE: I did not suggest that. I said, "Why not?"

Yes, the hon. member said, "Why not?" I was about to correct him when eleven o'clock came, and the right hon. Prime Minister suggested I should continue to-day. The reason I have not an answer to give him to the new proposal he made was that that which he had suggested was not the proposition laid down in the bill. The bill which we have before us dealt with Montmagny and L'Islet. Had the bill referred to Montmagny and Kamouraska it would have been a different proposition. However the proposition before us last night was that of joining up Montmagny and L'Islet, thereby taking away the Liberal majority of 585 votes.

Now that we have complied with the rules of the house I ask the indulgence of hon. members to proceed with the rest of my remarks in regard to the redistribution bill before us. When I was speaking this morning the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Moore) expressed a doubt when I said that in the proposed merger of the counties of Beauharnois and Laprairie an encroachment was being made on the county of Beauharnois in order to get around the small parish of St. Etienne, and to bring it into the county of Huntingdon. There is no doubt about the matter; I looked at the map to refresh my memory in regard to the point. There is no doubt in the world that the taking of the parish of St. Etienne from the county of Beauharnois
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

creates an encroachment on the county of Beauharnois, and creates a hole in the southern section of the constituency. If there is any doubt in the minds of hon. members I need only place before your eyes a map of what is going to be the county of Chateau-guay-Huntingdon. Anyone can see the white section at the right of the map I now hold in my hand. The part to which I am now directing the attention of hon. members is that part taken from the constituency of St. Johns-Iberville, That is the Lacolle section. The small white part at the top of this map is the parish of St. Etienne which is taken from the county of Beauharnois and is to be placed in the constituency of Chateauguay-Huntingdon. At the corner of this map there is the parish of Ste. Barbe which, according to the project, is taken from the constituency of Chateauguay-Huntingdon and put into the new constituency of Beauharnois-Laprairie. There is no doubt about my contention of this morning. Anything I have said is amply supported by the maps which have been prepared showing the different constituencies, and which have been distributed to all hon. members. I need only pass before the eyes of hon. members the map which I hold in my hand showing the new county of Beauharnois-Laprairie, including the corridor I mentioned, to prove my statement. I am placing before you a design of what is going to be the county of Beauharnois-Laprairie.

It
looks like a tape-worm.

This small section to which I am pointing is only about two miles wide. That is the corridor by means of which connection is established between the present counties of Laprairie and Beauharnois. I suggest that my contention of this morning is perfectly justified. Then hon. members will see the little hole which is taken out, and the little tail added by the addition of the parish of Ste. Barbe. That is the position. Surely no one would contend that this change has been made in order to give more seats to the city of Montreal. More seats could be given to that city without disturbing these two parishes. If we must unite the counties of Beauharnois and Laprairie I do not object so much. Please add them together, but do not take out of one county a certain parish which satisfies a group and leave out another section of the adjoining county. I think it is unfair, and this is enough to show what 
has been the spirit of those who have engineered the project of redistribution that we are dealing with at the present time.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I might be asked what would be the logical method of doing away with -the county of Beauharnois, which is a small constituency. The logical course- though I admit that there are difficulties and that several objections could be raised, not from the point of view of geography but other considerstions-rthe natural and logical course would be to join both Beauharnois and Chateauguaj'-Huntingdon. They are both part of the triangle which is formed by the St. Lawrence river, the American boundary and the counties of Laprairie and Napierville. This would be a perfect delimitation of the constituency. I recognize that it would make a very largely populated constituency, that is true. And there may be another objection of which I am ready to take cognizance. It would make that county an overwhelmingly Freneh-Canadian county, and my friends could raise the objection that an Englishspeaking constituency in the province of Quebec was 'being done away with. That is one of the reasons for my observation that this plan would be reasonable and logical but there are serious objections to it which we ought to take into- consideration, and to which I would be -the first to give due weight. It would be probably a too largely populated constituency, and as to the division between the English-speaking and the French-speaking communities, it might be unfair to the English-speaking minority of the province of Quebec. Therefore in that case we are forced to abandon the logical course, the reasonable course, and try to adjust the matter in some other way. If nothing better is offered I am ready to accept the establishment of a little corridor to join the counties of Beauharnois and Chateauguay and Laprairie, but I insist that these two counties be united in the position in which they are at the present time, that -they be not carved.
Now, Mr. Chairman, let us come to the next county which presents a serious difficulty, the county that my good friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) is trying to create for himself. He was elected in the riding of Chambly-Vercheres with a majority of nearly 1,200 at the last election. I am very much surprised that he is not ready to go and face the same electors again. Generally speaking the changes that he proposes to make are not going to help him to create a seat in the island of Montreal. The change of the limits

Redistribution-Mr. Cardin
of his constituency is for other reasons than finding another constituency in Montreal. He was elected in the riding of Chambly-Vercheres, and according to the new proposal he wants to make me a gift of the county of Vercheres. As far as that is concerned, and if I were the only one to be considered, I would be very much pleased. There is no better population in the whole of Canada than the population of the county of Vercheres. That population comes in a direct line from those who discovered this country and who first established Christianity in Canada. In the parishes of the county of Vercheres we find the best citizens and the best Canadians to be found anywhere in the Dominion. As far as I am concerned, personally, I would see no objection to taking them into my county or giving them to someone else who may replace me at the next general election. Why my hon. friend is abandoning that county of Vercheres I do not, I cannot understand. The reasons which have been given up to the present time are no reasons at all, they are not even a. pretence capable of justifying the scheme of the present bill. But my hon. friend wants to give me the county of Vercheres, excepting a section which he wants to keep with him in the county of Chambly. That section is that part of the county of Vercheres included in the municipality of the town of Beloeil, the village of McMasterville, and the municipalities of Ste. Julie and St. Mathieu. I frankly admit that when we discussed the matter before that solemn committee of elder statesmen I did not raise any great objection to that. I wanted to accommodate the Minister of Marine; his summer residence is in the town of Beloeil and in view of that fact I was ready to concede that he might keep part of the county of Vercheres.
