I mention this fact only to show in what way the work of preparing this plan of redistribution has been organized. This is an illustration of the ideas that prevailed; it shows very clearly the desire of those who are the masters and who prepared that redistribution. But the Minister of Marine is not satisfied with leaving out of his constituency the county of Vercheres; he wants to carve from the county of Laprairie a small section, a small community which is at present in that county and which is to be added to the county of Chambly to satisfy his desire. He said: Well, it does not amount to much, it is a small territory. If it does not amount to much why not respect the limits of the county of Laprairie and not go to the expense and
trouble of encroaching on it by taking that small and unimportant section to add to the county of Chambly? He wants to replace the county of Vercheres-which apparently he does not like because he wants to get rid of it-by the county of Rouville. There would not be so much objection if he wanted to take the whole county of Rouville, but no. He wants to cross over the river. They do not like to cross over rivers in other sections of the province, they want to make the rivers the boundaries, but my hon. friend is not afraid to go over the Richelieu river and to take part of the county of Rouville, a part in which he expects to be a little more successful than he was in the county of Vercheres which he wants to detach from his constituency. If he wanted to take the whole county of Rouville, well and good. If he wanted to replace the county of Vercheres by the county of Rouville in its entirety I would agree to that.
The whole or nothing.

But his objection is that that would make too large a population. He said: With what I have to-day, with what has been carved out for me, I have 40,000 population. If he would take the rest of the county of Rouville that he refuses and leave the part of Vercheres he wants to retain, the population would come within a reasonable figure. But he does not want to take the whole county of Rouville for reasons which are obvious. There is a section in that county where he might be very successful and there is another section in which his success would be rather doubtful at the present time and under present circumstances. Mr. Chairman, I think that that is not fair. Our complaints in regard to the situation are perfectly justified. To repeat what I said this morning, Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand why the Conservative members, including the ministers, who were elected in 1930 are afraid to go back to the electors who sent them here. Certain members on the other side of the house deserve credit and praise for their courage. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) is ready to go back to his constituency as it existed in 1930; the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) is also ready to face the constituents he faced in 1930, and the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) is ready to do the same. This is a good example which should be followed by the two French Canadian ministers from the district of Montreal. Neither my good friend the Minister of
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

Marine (Mr. Duranleau) nor my good friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) is ready to go before the electors by whom he was elected in 1930; each minister wants his constituency changed. Apparently these hon. gentlemen have not the courage that is possessed by the hon. members for Stanstead, Compton and Brome-Missisquoi.
That is the position, Mr. Chairman, and I say there is no justification in the world for the proposal which has been made with regard to the new constituency of Chambly-Rou-ville. That is not the proper name for it; if it were named according to the division which has been suggested it should be called Cha-mbly-Rouville-Vercheres-Laprairie. That should be the name of the new constituency which has -been carved out for the benefit of my good friend the Minister of Marine. This is most objectionable, and in order to bring about that result the riding of Riehelieu-Vercheres must be composed of the old county of Richelieu, plus a section of Yercheres, plus a section of the county of St. Hyacinthe, and a portion of the county of Yamaska. This is the sort of constituency that is being created mder this redistribution. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that it does not mean very much, but if that is so why not keep them as they are at the present time? That would cause less embarrassment and would indicate a little more confidence on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite in the electors whom they will have to face in a year or two.
I have dealt with the constituency of Richelieu-Vercheres, Mr. Chairman; now let us go to the constituency of Nicolet-Yamaska. Because of its small population the county of Tamaska is bound to disappear. It has been kept with a small population for many years, when circumstances permitted the keeping of small constituencies, such as Argenteuil with only 18,000 and Richelieu with only 21,000. That county of Yamaska, I repeat, we are practically agreed should disappear, but in my humble judgment it should disappear in a reasonable, fair and logical way. This is a small constituency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Yes, about 17,000 at the
present time. Why not add this constituency to Richelieu or Nicolet, or even Bagot? I see my right hon. friend the Prime Minister smiling when I mention Richelieu; probably he is under the impression that this would make Richelieu a pretty safe seat for me. If taat is what my right hon. friend has in mind let me tell him that with the carving they have done they have made my seat
[Mr. Card in.1
much safer than it would be with Yamaska added to it; so I do not need to be placed in such a position. They are giving me a very strong Conservative section of St. Hyacinthe; if I have to take these people I shall be glad to do so, because they are very good citizens, though it will mean a majority of more than 400 against me there. By this means they are bringing my constituency to the very door of the city of St. Hyacinthe; that is the situation in which I find myself. However, it has been thought desirable to unite the county of Yamaska with the county of Nicolet. Very well; we can agree on that, but unite it as a whole; do not destroy the old county of Nicolet.
Let me deal first with the section of the county of Yamaska which is near the county of Richelieu. The proposal in the bill is that the municipality of Yamaska be cut in two; one half is to be united with the county of Richelieu-because they are Liberals-and the balance is to be added to the county of Nicolet. That is the sort of work that is being done. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that the Yamaska river runs through that territory. That river goes through the municipality of Yamaska; they are not separate municipalities on each side. The Yamaska river is not a navigable stream; it is narrow, and at present there is a highway bridge connecting the two parts of the municipality. My hon. friends may answer, though it is not an answer, that in certain other places -municipalities have been divided. Well, two wrongs never make a right, and if that anomaly exists somewhere else that is no reason why the same thing should be done this year.	The municipality of	Yamaska
should not be separated into two sections.
Now let us come to the county of Nicolet. Is it proposed to keep that county as it is? No; in joining the greater part of Yamaska with the county of Nicolet they want to do away with six old parishes of the old county of Nicolet and throw them into the county	of	Lotbiniere.	They	want tocarve that new constituency at both ends; adjoining the county of Richelieu they want to cut the municipality of Yamaska in two, and where the county of Nicolet touches the county of Lotbiniere they want to take away six parishes and include them in Lotbiniere. They want	to	-hive those	people	with theLiberals in	the	county of	Lotbiniere. My
hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) said we should not complain if anything is done to make the Liberal seat of Lotbiniere safer. Hon. gentlemen opposite want to make it extra safe; they want to include in

Redistribution-Mr. Cardin
the county of Lotbiniere the Liberal parishes of the county of Nicolet. That is the sort of gerrymander that is proposed.
I have heard hon. members mention municipal lines and provincial lines, and I have even heard arguments based on what are called diocesan lines; that is, that we should not destroy the limits of the diocese of a bishop. By doing that you are destroying the diocese of the Bishop of Nicolet at both ends, taking six of his parishes in Nicolet and throwing them into the county of Lotbiniere.
I do not insist so much upon that because I realize the force of the argument that the federal constituencies should be constructed having in view federal exigencies. I refer to this circumstance however to answer certain arguments which have been advanced against concessions that have been refused in certain quarters of the province of Quebec. If these two counties of Yamaska and Nicolet are to be joined they should be joined as they are without being carved at both ends, as now proposed.
Before leaving the southern section of the St. Lawrence, let me say a word or two in regard to the counties of Richmond-Wolfe. The counties in the eastern townships have not been touched generally; that was the understanding, the idea which prevailed at first when the party in power prepared the bill. Stanstead is not disturbed; Sherbrooke is not disturbed; Compton is not disturbed; Shef-ford is not disturbed. Why then disturb the old counties of Richmond-Wolfe?

May I put a question to the hon. member?
Mr. CARDIN (Translation); Certainly.

Have you taken into account the population of these various counties? The county of Richmond-Wolfe has a larger population than any other county in the eastern townships. Did you compare the figures of the population of these various counties with those of Richmond-Wolfe? Richmond-Wolfe has a population of 41,867 while those of the neighbouring counties vary between 25,000 and 31,000. Richmond-W'olfe is the most populated constituency in the eastern townships and I consider that it is only fair and just that part, of its population be transferred. That is what I wished to point out to the hon. member and the house.

I quite understand the
observations which the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe is making. His argument is
that the county as it stands at the present time has a larger population than the counties I have just mentioned in the eastern townships. But if that is the case, if his county is too large and if others are too small, why not increase the small ones? I am not the master of this redistribution; the government is the father of the bill. If the member for Stanstead has not a sufficient population why not increase it? If there is not a sufficient population in Compton-if I am not mistaken the figure is 29,000, but it does not matter -and if the county of Stanstead is too small, a county of 25,000, why not have an increase to a certain extent? If that were done we might find a justification for taking out from the counties of Richmond-Wolfe a certain proportion of their population. The idea that has been put forward since this discussion has started has been to increase the population of small counties. Why then reduce counties which are still below the number they should have according to the census? If my hon. friend's county of Richmond-Wolfe has 42,000, it is still lower than the figure which is given as a guide for redistribution. Why not keep as they are counties which have a reasonable population at the present time and so avoid the necessity next time of going over all these constituencies again, exposing them to changes as a result of every census? If the county of Richmond-Wolfe has 40,000 it is within the reasonable limits of population, and the county is not going to be disturbed by the next census; \?hereas if you reduce the county of Richmond-Wolfe to a population of 30,000 or 29,000, at the next census you will have to recast the whole thing and bring in a new scheme of redistribution. I understand my hon. friend's position, but a county with a population of 40,000 is not extraordinary, because one of the new counties being created in the north of the province of Quebec is to be established with a population of 41,000; and there are in the province of Quebec a number of constituencies which are not being touched and in which the population is higher than the population in the county of Richmond-Wolfe. One has only to look at the counties of Drummond-Arthabaska, 53.000;' Charlevoix-Saguenay, 55,000; Chambly-Rou-ville, as at present carved, 40,000; and there are many others in the same position. Pontiac has 42,000, Rimouski 40,000, and St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, as now proposed, will have a population of 42,000.

Have you any objection to mentioning the counties which have less population?
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

I have no
objection, absolutely none.
I have not gone through the list, but I admit, and it is undeniable, that there are several counties with a much smaller population than Richmond-Wolfe. I am not blind; I can realize that, and I know perfectly well that there are other counties in that situation. But I think I am equally right in saying that there is no reason for complaint on the ground that the population of the county is 40,000 when the present bill creates new constituencies in rural Quebec with a population exceeding that figure, and when by this bill we are increasing the population of certain small constituencies where the figure is lower than 40,000.
In my opinion therefore it is not fair to bring about such a change without the necessity for providing a new seat. This has no relation whatever to the creation of new seats in Montreal-none at all. The changes I have just mentioned affect only the relationship between counties and counties and do not help to provide one more county for Montreal or in the north of the province of Quebec. I think it is unfair to take away from Richmond-Wolfe five or six parishes which have always been included in that county.
The Solicitor General referred, as no doubt other hon. members will, to the changes made in 1924. May I point out that in the proposed changes in this redistribution bill there is nothing to alter what was done in 1924. If there is any complaint in regard to the changes made in 1924 it cannot be of any great importance because hon. gentlemen are ready to accept what was done at that time. Their proposed changes do not reestablish the limits before 1924. The changes that are being made are new ones, absolutely independent of the changes which were made in the redistribution of 1924, so that on that score there is no justification for hon. gentlemen opposite. They may cite a list of changes in 1924, most of them minor changes, and to which no one objected, but the proof that everything was satisfactory is the fact that hon. gentlemen were elected in 1930 on the strength of that redistribution. And they are not asking that a change be made now.
I am frank enough and fair enough to say that if the committee of elder statesmen had continued to sit I could have reached an agreement with the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe. I think he knows me well enough to understand that I would have been fair and I believe we could have found common ground upon which to agree with regard 
to Richmond-Wolfe. I submit that it is not fair that this thing should be done in the
way it is being done by this bill. After all, this would have been a very small difficulty to adjust between ourselves. I know he is fair enough and I think he will credit me with also being fair. He may not have been the master of the situation but perhaps we could have gone over the head of somebody else and found ground for agreement in regard to this county. A constituency is being dismantled without justification. So much for the southern section of the province of Quebec.
Let us go north for a moment. The proposal made by this bill is that the counties of L'Assomption and Terrebonne be joined. Terrebonne is a large county and it does not need to be increased. Its population is larger than that of many of the constituencies which have been created by this redistribution bill. Terrebonne could be left without being disturbed because it has sufficient population. I submit it is a mistake to change the present constituency of L'Assomption-Montcalm. These counties were united by the Conservative party in 1914 and they go together better than any other two counties in Canada. They have common interests in the cultivation of tobacco, one of the most important industries in the dominion, and the addition of Terrebonne will change the whole situation. But if this has to be done, why should it not be done by joining L'Assomption and Terrebonne in their entirety. Why does the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) want to carve out of the county of Terrebonne the towns of Ste. Therese and St. Janvier? Why not leave these two places where they are; why disturb the boundaries of Terrebonne? Terrebonne could have been joined to L'Assomption to provide another constituency to take care of Montreal or the northern section of the province. But they were not satisfied to do that. They have created a riding which will cause some difficulties when considered from certain points of view. Instead of separating L'Assomption and Montcalm, I think we would be ready to join with Joliette, not only Montcalm but also L'Assomption. It is true that that would make a very large constituency but the county of Joliette-
We are willing to accept the hon. member's offer.

Without any restrictions? I have heard that a proposal of that kind would be permitted to go through provided we allowed the Postmaster General to get

Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau
Ste. Therese and St. Janvier. Other centres would be thrown into Montreal. That cannot be agreed to but if they want to avoid dividing the counties of L'Assomption and Montcalm and join them with the county of Joliette, as far as we are concerned we are inclined to agree. It would make a constituency with a little over 50$00 of population but we would not be afraid of that. There are other constituencies in the province containing more than 50,000 population. I have mentioned one already which contains 55,000.
I regret that I must abide by the forty-mdnute rule but I will complete my observations after another hon. gentleman has spoken.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as was stated
this morning by some hon. members on this side of the house, this redistribution was not desired by the party in power. It had to be done according to our constitution. At every decennial census it is the duty of parliament to redistribute the representation in the House of Commons. I think everyone will admit that redistribution is a very difficult task. The adjusting of boundaries of constituencies is a difficult problem and it is natural that diversities of opinion exist on the subject. It is manifestly impossible to make a division which will please everyone but after having heard my hon. friends opposite one would come to the conclusion that they want no redistribution at all. They want the boundaries of the counties left exactly as they are; they do not want to consider the changes in population and other circumstances which should be taken into consideration in a case like this. I was not a member of the committee but I have studied the map and the figures suggested by the committee and in my opinion it is a very fair redistribution. This committee has taken into consideration every circumstance which should be considered. Our friends opposite seem to have only one thing in mind-political circumstances.
Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
If a parish or a township has been taken from one county and put into another my hon. friends opposite will not admit that the committee had to take into consideration the equality of population. They say it has been for political purposes. I am not surprised to hear those views because our friends opposite have had their own way in the province of Quebec for forty years. They have ruled in that province, they have made
their own political map and decided their own boundaries, provincially and municipally. As everyone knows, the political map of Quebec is the basis of redistribution in the federal field. Of course, if you look at the statutes of Canada you will not find many changes except perhaps in 1903. I might come to that later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Not during the debate on this redistribution.
I shall be ready to meet the hon. gentleman on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: A number of changes were made in 1903 and if many were not made in 1924, this was because the basis of our redistribution was the provincial boundaries. Our friends from Quebec who are not very scrupulous and I think the Dillon act, which is still on the statutes of Quebec, is a proof that they were not very scrupulous-

I
rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has accused us on this side of not being scrupulous. I suggest that that is not parliamentary and should not be used.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Speaking to the point of order, I just stated that the Quebec boundaries were made the basis of the federal redistribution and I am trying to show that the lines of those boundaries were not very scrupulously made.
It was not the boundaries the hon. member said were not scrupulous; it was the men who made the boundaries that he said were not scrupulous. That is unparliamentary and should not be used.

Boundaries
have no scruples.
The hon. member did not name any member; I think he is in order.
He named the members on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our hon. friends
opposite are asking why so many changes in the province of Quebec have been made by the redistribution committee. Obviously, if we wanted to make a fair redistribution we had to make these changes. As has been stated, we had to give three more seats to the island of Montreal and on account of the in-
Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau

crease in population from 36,000, the quota of representation of the last distribution, to a quota this year of 44,100, we could not do otherwise than make changes. Then we have to take into consideration the fact that our hon. friends opposite in the redistribution of 1924 did not seem to take into account the population of the province. Why? Was it because they were satisfied politically with the lines of the constituencies in Quebec in 1924 when they had friends returned in almost every riding? Was it because of that that they left a great number of seats in Quebec with a population of 20,000 although the quota was 36,000? Why did they do that?
Hon. gentlemen opposite have done the same thing this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Do they not think the duty of parliament in case of redistribution is to take into consideration the population of the province, not the fact that a constituency is Liberal and that a change might affect the chances of a Liberal friend? We have to take into consideration the population of every constituency and that is what has been done in this instance. The hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) admitted very frankly that it was a difficult task to make a redistribution so as to give to the population equality of representation. He stated that in Quebec we were anxious to preserve a few seats for the English speaking element of our province. I am quite in accord with my hon. friend's views on this question. It is true that we have always been trying to give to the minority in Quebec a fair representation in this house and I think this should be the case in all the provinces; every minority should have a voice in the House of Commons and that is why we have protected some of the English-speaking constituencies of Quebec.
The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Richelieu have laid great stress on the provincial or municipal boundaries of the constituencies of our province. According to them, it is a crime for this house to touch these boundaries.
It is not a crime; it is a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Why do they say so? We do not deprive those citizens of their right of voting; we do not deprive them of the rights of citizenship. They have still the right to vote and I say that we give that population an opportunity to be in a better position to exercise their rights of citizenship than was the case before. We have to take into consideration the population of those constituencies. 
To my hon. friends who are so fond of speaking about respecting the municipal boundaries of Quebec, I say: That is fine to hear, but was it done in the past by the Liberal party?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If you read the Hansards of the past, $ou will find the principles which were laid down by the late great chief of the Liberal party in regard to the lines of municipal counties in Quebec, but what did they do after the speech of their leader on the subject?
They did right.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Under my hon. friends there were in Quebec twenty-three federal constituencies, also provincial constituencies, which did not conform to municipal lines.
May I say just a word to my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If my hon. friend wishes to make a speech, I shall not allow it, but if it a question, it is all right.
Just one sentence and it will be short. In the province of Quebec there have been changes pro forma, not to change but to maintain the old boundaries; that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend should wait to make those statements in one of his sixty-five speeches. That is not a question.
But this was a speech in one sentence.
What was the date when that statement was made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: During the session of 1899.
What date?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not the date, but I can give the volume of Hansard and the page.
There was no redistribution that year.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There was the principle laid down by the Liberal party, but it was not followed. My hon. friends are like the reprobates of the Divine Comedy of Dante who left all their hopes at the door of the inferno. The Liberal party, before entering what they think is the heaven of power, leave at the door all their principles, to take them up again when they go out of power.

Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau
Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated that principle when he said:
We think it is a principle which will commend itself universally to public opinion, that the basis of representation in this house should be municipal and county organizations.
After quoting the words of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the leader of the opposition in 1924 said:
It is upon that basis-
Municipal organizations.
-we shall expect the committee to whom the present bill will be referred to proceed.
If you look at the Quebec map you will find that there are twenty-three constituencies in Quebec, provincially and federally, which do not conform to municipal boundaries or county boundaries. Take Arthabaska, Brome, Compton, Drummond, Frontenac, Hochelaga, Hull, Jacques Cartier, Kamouraska, Labelle, Lotbiniere, Matane, Megantic, Nicolet, Richmond, Rimouski, Saguenay, Stanstead, and Temiscouata-those counties are not the same as are the municipal counties. Why? Because the Liberal party did not follow that principle. I say that owing to a lack of redistribution made in 1924, a great number of constituencies were left without any quota. The redistribution at this time has to be made complete, and that is what we are doing. It is no crime to depart from municipal boundaries-not at all. I think it fair that we give to the population, irrespective of municipal boundaries, a fair representation in population and in area. It is well known that in arranging the redistribution we had to take into account a great number of circumstances.
The 'hon. member for Richelieu has dwelt at length with almost every constituency in the vicinity of Montreal. After listening to this gentleman we are supposed to believe that this redistribution is a terrible piece of legislation, that it is a monster, that it is anything that is bad. Well, Mr. Chairman, I say that exactly the contrary is true. If hon. members would look at the map and consider all the circumstances which have to be considered in connection with a redistribution, they will realize that the report of the committee is fair and equitable to every citizen in all parts of the country.
The hon. member has spoken about two new constituencies which were made in the northern part of the province. One has about 21,000 population and the other about 25,000 or 26,000. The two to which he has referred are Lafleche-St. Maurice and Chapleau. If the hon. member would look at the map he would see that Chapleau represents almost one-fifth of the whole area of the province of Quebec.

One of the areas has a
population of 46,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Chapleau represents
practically one-fifth of the area of the province of Quebec. Its population is not centred in small towns, but is scattered throughout the constituency. I hold that this constituency, which is crossed only by a railway, is entitled to representation. The citizens in that district could not be fairly represented with the map as it previously existed. Anyone who is familiar with the province will admit that some representation should be given to that part of the province. It is a section under colonization. I do not say that the population will increase rapidly but I do say that owing to the area and the population that constituency should 'have a representative.
The same observations would apply to Lafleche-St. Maurice. It is a very large constituency with a large population. If hon. members would look at the figures they would conclude that a fairly reasonable division has been made. The hon. member has suggested that a change has been made in connection with Three Rivers in order that an easier seat would be made for the hon. member for Three Rivers-St. Maurice (Mr. Bourgeois). But if my hon. friend would consider all the circumstances I believe he would change his mind and come to the conclusion that this redistribution has been fair and equitable.
My hon. friend spoke concerning the divisions in the city of Montreal. Both parties agreed that instead of giving thirteen seats to that city it would be only fair that with a population of over 1,006,000 people it should be entitled to at least sixteen representatives, with a quota of 50,000 to 75,000 representation. My hon. friend asked why a redivision should be made of all the constituencies in the city of Montreal. I hold such a change was absolutely necessary.

That is not exactly what
I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
We could not add
three new seats to Montreal without retouching almost every constituency on the island. My hon. friend's own maps would show the same thing. Hon. members opposite admitted it had to be done. Hon. members say that the constituency of St. Mary has disappeared. Speaking frankly, I do not see anything in that. St. James, St. Mary, Hochelaga and Maisonneuve all have about the same population. It is a population of Canadians with large families, aspirations, people with the same habits. I do not see any crime in making a slight difference in the boundary lines. The only way to do it was to put St. James
Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau

and St. Mary in one constituency. I say there was nothing wrong in that. As a matter of fact my hon. friend will admit that we were prepared to meet their wishes. We were prepared to give to St. Mary the very same lines which existed previously, although to my mind it made no difference at all. We were and are still prepared to do that. I say that my hon. friends are now trying to make some political capital out of this matter of redistribution. If I judge correctly from the tone of their speeches made this morning, that would seem to be their object.
My hon. friend spoke also of Outre-mont. I am glad he brought up this question. When the first draft was made by the committee my hon. friend representing Laurier strenuously objected to the lines of the city of Outremont being changed. Is that right or not?
All the division. I wanted Outremont to remain as it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That was the wish of my hon. friend. Now that we are reverting to the lines of the city of Outremont, my hon. friend seems to object.
Will my hon. friend allow me a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I want to put that question to my hon. friend and when answering he might put his own question. Do I understand that my hon. friend representing Laurier-Outremont is now opposing the line of the city of Outremont? I want to know that, because we can accommodate my hon. friend otherwise. But I say this: if we have reverted to the line of the city of Outremont it is because it was the wish of my hon. friend at first and because it is the wish of a great number of citizens of that part of the constituency.

The question that I wanted to put to the minister is this: will he explain exactly what is to be done with Montreal? We have heard so many rumours we do not know where we are. If the minister would say now what is to be done to Montreal that might clarify the situation and there might not be any discussion at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I do not intend at the present time to give all the details of the redistribution in the island of Montreal, it would take too long. It will come in committee when we discuss each and every constituency in the island of Montreal. But I

thought it was the wish of my hon. friend that we should revert to the city lines, and that is what we are doing. Anyway we will come to this point later. Now my hon. friend from Richelieu said: Why touch the lines of the counties in the city of Montreal?
That is not what I said. My hon. friend ought to be fair. I said: Why change the agreement practically reached before the special committee of what is called the elder statesmen?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Because we did not agree.

We were satisfied, we
agreed.
We might agree now, but we do not know where we stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If you do not know now you will know later on. But I may say our friends in Quebec have changed the boundaries of the counties in the island of Montreal time and again. My hon. friends will remember 1923 when my county of Laurier was cut in half to make a Liberal constituency, which is called to-day the Mercier division.
That was not federal.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
No, but I say our friends opposite did not respect county boundaries at all. They divided the counties to fit their own purposes, their political purposes. It is surprising to see how scandalized and amazed they are to-day because we have made some redistribution to give a fair representation to the population of Quebec.
My hon. friends have dwelt at some length on the new constituency of Chateauguay-Huntingdon and Beauhamois-Laprairie. Well, I suppose my hon. friend will not complain of the fact that we have left Vaudreuil-Soulanges with 21,000 population without any change whatever. I suppose my hon. friend will not object to that?
And Laprairie will have to pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend has studied the situation carefully, when he makes that statement.
I know one thing, my riding is cut away.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
At first we thought that Beauhamois should be united to Vaudreuil-Soulanges. Of course everyone knows

Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau
that Vaudreuil-Soulanges is on the boundary of Ontario, no population can be taken from that side. Vaudreuil-Soulanges have about the same population as Beauharnois; the church interests are the same, their bishop is at Valley-field, they have their courts at Valleyfield and they go to Valleyfield for their business-

Not at all. I come from Valleyfield, there is no bridge,
there is no communication.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is a railway bridge.
Two trains a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: And apart from a little portion on one side of the lake the river St. Lawrence is not very large there, and not deep at all. As a matter of fact we all know-
You cannot walk across, there is enough water to prevent you walking.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, but you have the railway bridge.
Do you see the farmer with his cart crossing on the railway bridge? He would be killed by the train.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend is very cute.
The farmer would not be so cute.
Your proposition is more cute.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The proposition was fair, it would give a population of from 40,000 to 42,000. But my hon. friends objected so strenuously that we had to yield and say, all right, we will not touch Vaudreuil-Soulanges. But the committee had to do something with the other constituencies. I admit it was a very difficult task, not because we wanted to make a Conservative constituency, my hon. friends opposite will admit that Vaudreuil-Soulanges is a Liberal constituency, and my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) will admit that Laprairie and Beauharnois will be a Liberal constituency. I do not think there is any question about that. When my hon. friend speaks of the corridor, I say exactly the contrary; there is a corridor existing now and we are doing away with that corridor by joining Laprairie and Beauharnois. If you take the map you will see that Chateauguay-Huntingdon is on the boundary of the United States, down -below.
Down below!

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, my expression may not be appropriate. I hope my hon. friend will be happier in his expressions when he will address the house. I say that a part of Chateauguay goes as high as the St. Lawrence river perhaps three or four miles or more, while Chateauguay-Huntingdon goes as far as the St. Lawrence river, starting from the United States boundary. The committee thought the only thing to do was to use that strip of land as a connecting link between Beauhamois-Laprairie. It makes a very reasonable constituency. I do not say it is perfect, it is impossible to make things perfect under these circumstances, but they have the population. If you look at the figures you will see that they have a fairly good representation, 41,399. Now you have the national route starting from Montreal to Malone which passes through these two constituencies. As a matter of fact the future representative of Beauharnois-Laprairie will visit his whole constituency in a day on account of that national road. The population of both constituencies have the same habits and the same interests.
We are not a band of Zulus!

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend can object very strenuously to the joining of these constituencies.
They hear the same things on the radio.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend from Richelieu admits that in these circumstances the joining of those two counties would be accepted, except the removing of St. Etienne and Ste. Barbe from -one constituency to another. My hon. friend made a good deal of fuss about those two parishes. Well, I think if you look at the map you will see that these two parishes are on the edge of the constituencies, and the change does not destroy the lines materially.
The minister is not serious, surely, when he makes that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
One of our 'hon.
friends opposite said that since the report of the committee the map of Quebec has been a sort of puzzle. Well, Mr. Chairman, the map of Quebec has been a puzzle for years. My hon. friends had their own way in that province, and I would invite our Englishspeaking friends from the other provinces to look at the map of Quebec as it was after the redistribution of 1924. The map is nothing but a puzzle, and if you look at the map to-day you will see that it is much better.

Still worse.
Redistribution-Mr. Duranleau

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The map is at the
disposal of my hon. friends; my hon. friend from Temiscouata knows it very well.
I know the map by heart, as well as the minister does.
What about the Indian reservation near Caughnawaga? You are getting away with that if you leave it in Beauharnois.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It forms part of La-prairie, and it is not disturbed.

Do those
Indians go into Chambly?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, not at all. I will come to that in a moment; there is nothing extraordinary about my own constituency. My hon. friend from Richelieu said there was only one thing to do, and that was to join Beauharnois with Chateauguay-Huntingdon.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That was what I
understood; if I am wrong I should like to be corrected.
I said that could be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend admitted that it would be quite proper.

No, I said it could be
done; geographically that would be the best thing, but there are other objections.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
admit that if this had been done it would have been a departure from the principle that, so far as possible, we should protect the seats of the minority.
I said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
If Beauharnois had
been joined to Chateauguay-Huntingdon it would have nullified the chances of an English candidate in that constituency.
That was one of the objections I mentioned as against the geographical advantages.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend made particular reference to the division of Chambly-Rouville and St. Hyacinthe and Richelieu. That was also a very difficult problem with regard to population. As my hon. friend knows, Richelieu had a representation of only 21,000. Surely we could not have Vaudreuil-Soulanges with a population of only 21,000 and Richelieu with the same population as well, so the committee thought that a division should be made in order to give a fair representation in population to

Richelieu. This is why the larger part of Vercheres was joined to Richelieu. My hon. friend says the member for Chambly-Ver-cheres was not satisfied with the citizens of Vercheres. I can tell my hon. friend that I have more friends in Vercheres to-day than in any other part of the province; I have no better friends than those in Vercheres. The committee did not only consider the interests of the member; we had to give fair representation according to population, and that is why the committee thought a part of Vercheres should be added to Richelieu.
My hon. friend went to to say that a part of Laprairie was also added to Chambly. I am afraid my hon. friend does not know the conditions existing there. As a matter of fact that was done against my wish. The committee asked me if I would consent to take a strip of land in Laprairie because the population of St. Lambert and Greenfield Park, which are two cities on the bounaries of Laprairie, had overflowed. This overflow formed part of Greenfield Park and St. Lambert so far as religious purposes and other interests are concerned, as a matter of fact a part of this population is called St. Lambert annex. I was asked, and the committee was asked by some citizens of that locality, if there would be any objection to joining this little strip of land to the population of St. Lambert and Greenfield Park because as a matter of fact they had nothing to do with Laprairie except to pay taxes there. All their relations were with St. Lambert and Greenfield Park. I said I had no objection, but personally I do not care whether or not I keep that part of Laprairie that is added to Chambly.
Will the minister allow me a question? Who gave him this information that these people had nothing to do with Laprairie?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to ask the committee about that, but I know that someone representing that population came to the committee and asked if this would not be advisable. The population only numbers a little over 700, so it is not very important. They claim that all their relations are with St. Lambert and with Greenfield Park.
The hon. gentleman has spoken for forty minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Would not my hon.
friend admit that these three parishes on the other side of the bridge practically form part of the island of Montreal?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Are not the residents of these three parishes almost all citizens of Montreal-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -having their place of business in Montreal.
That is not the case. These municipalities have formed part of the county of Two Mountains for years.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: But now there is the overflow in Montreal.

You object to taking into the county of Nicolet and Yamaska the western section of the village of Yamaska because there is the river of Yamaska, and now you want to throw across Riviere des Prairies the three parishes I have mentioned and which are now in Two Mountains. If you wish to keep Yamaska river as the boundary in one case, you ought to keep Riviere des Prairies as the boundary in the other, as it has been for years. These municipalities are not inhabited by citizens of Montreal; they are municipalities and centres by themselves and the population lives there the year round. There is no comparison between these three centres and other centres along lake St. Louis in the county of Jacques Cartier. These people are summer residents, in the section of Dorval and along St. Louis in the constituency of Jacques Cartier; but L'Abord a Plouffe and Laval des Rapides have always been in the county of Two Mountains, and there is no more objection to their being in the county of Two Mountains because they are small villages than there is to the town of Ste. Therese. If the minister wants to discard these centres because they are villages, why does the Postmaster General want to take Ste. Therese from the county of Terrebonne and place it in the county of Two Mountains? In my opinion there is no justification for such a proposal.
The proposal before us now is to increase the county of Argenteuil, which at the present time-

It has been settled
this afternoon.

I am not speaking of
what has transpired since negotiations took place. In the bill before us it is suggested that the county of Argenteuil should be increased by taking the southeast corner of the county of Labelle and transferring it into the county of Argenteuil, building up the population from 18,000 to about 28,000 in the
Redialribution-Mr. Cardin

county of Argenteuil. But there is no need to destroy the county of Labelle as it exists. That county should remain as it is. There is no reason for making such a change. The population of the county of Labelle is not very large, but it is larger than the population of surrounding counties, and if the county of Labelle is large enough, the county of Argenteuil being a small county, why arrange matters in such a way that, instead of having a large county and a small one, we shall have two small counties now? If you take that part of the county of Labelle and place it in the county of Argenteuil, Argenteuil will still be a small county and you will only make the county of Labelle smaller than it is at present. There is no reason for such a change. It would be easy to make adjustments in Argenteuil. It could be joined to Terrebonne, which would be logical. The more logical step to take, from the point of view of population and boundaries, would be to join Argenteuil to Two Mountains; they are two small counties. But I am fair enough to recognize that it is probably asking too much to propose that you place two ministers together, one in front of the other. Throwing the hon. member for Argenteuil into a fight with the Postmaster General would be logical, taking into consideration the constituencies, the boundary lines and the population; but it might not be fair so far as personal feelings are concerned. Therefore I do not insist on that. I mention it only to show what would be the more logical thing to do, joining two counties that have not sufficient population if they remain as they are. You might also join the county of Two Mountains and the county of Terrebonne; that would be much more logical than joining L'Assomption and Terrebonne. There are many ways whereby the difficulty might be adjusted. I will go further. If the government is ready to join together L'Assomption, Montcalm and Joli-ette, I am prepared to leave all the other constituencies in that vicinity undisturbed- no change in Terrebonne, no change in Two Mountains, no change in Argenteuil, no change in the county of Labelle. So far as I am concerned, I would just as soon leave the county of Argenteuil as it is; it is an English speaking constituency with a population of 18,000, and I would just as soon have it that way as with 25,000 or 26,000 or even 28,000 because it would still be a small constituency. It would still be too small a constituency and any readjustment in population would not improve matters very much.
I think we could all agree and leave the rest of the northern section of the province as 
it is. That would be a very satisfactory settlement. I would not be afraid to have in the province of Quebec certain constituencies where the population was below the required number. It would not matter very much because whatever we do we cannot equalize the population in that province. That is impossible, so what is the use of carving out of a constituency a certain number of parishes in order to increase the ad-' joining constituency by a small number? The result is that even with the addition, the population has not been brought up to the number required by the last census. What is the use of disturbing all the harmony which has existed in that section of the province in order to achieve a result which is not better than the present situation? Let, if you will, Joliette have a population of 51,000, and do not disturb the rest. I think that compromise could be accepted.
This completes my poor observations and I ask to be pardoned for having spoken so long with regard to this matter. I may have something to say later on but I want to conclude with the expression of a thought which is very deep in my heart, that we should b,e capable of doing better than has been done by this bill. We should be capable of stopping this disgraceful fight about small things which are not going to mean very much or have a very great significance when we place our arguments before the electors of the province of Quebec. I hate to see the province of Quebec made the subject of such criticism and such fighting. According to the information I have received, this will be the only province in which there will be a bitter fight to the end. Concessions have been made by the government in other provinces in order to reach an agreement and avoid disgraceful discussion in the House of Commons. Why are our Conservative friends from the province of Quebec not ready to make some concessions and put a little water in their wine in order that our province may not be held up as a disgrace? WThy should we show the public that we are incapable of understanding, Why should we fight over little things like the taking of a parish of less than 200 out of the county of Huntingdon, or a parish of a few hundred out of the county of Beauhar-nois? These are small things when compared with the problems with which the Prime Minister has to deal. A few parishes have been taken out of the county of Nicolet and put into the riding of Lotbiniere in order to make the former a safer ground for a Conservative candidate. It is considered that he would have a better chance but how does that com-

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
pare with the problems which we have to solve in these times of difficulty? What is that compared to the good reputation of the province of Quebec? These small matters could be disposed of and the bill could be corrected with five strokes of the pen. This could be done if we were reasonable on all sides and if our friends were willing to make legitimate concessions. I feel sure in the bottom of my heart that we can agree. Why should such a poor example be set for all the other provinces of Canada? Sacrifices have been made there by both sides of politics but in the province of Quebec we cannot agree.
Our friends on the other side want to take a small parish from Huntingdon to place it in Beauharnois; they want to put certain parishes in Chateauguay-Huntingdon and they want to take the Liberal parishes from Richmond-Wolfe and put them in Megantic.
I think I can see my way clear to speak for the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Lafleche) and say that they will make a compromise. There is a difference only of five or six parishes. I would be willing to cut that difference in two and give my hon. friend some satisfaction. I would do the same thing with the six parishes in Nicolet which it is proposed shall be thrown into Lotbiniere. I would be willing to make a sacrifice of three and possibly four in order to reach an agreement. These are some of the sacrifices I would be willing to make as a Liberal and as the leader of a very small section of the province of Quebec. I am ready to make these concessions in order to avoid1 the disgrace which is going to fall on the province of Quebec because we cannot agree.
Very serious sacrifices have been made in the province of Ontario in order to solve the difficulties there. I know it has not been an easy matter to have certain counties in Ontario kept as they are; I know it has been a very hard job for the hon. members who got together to keep the constituencies as they exist at the present time, but sacrifices have been made by the English speaking colleagues of the French ministers. I am told that sacrifices have been made in the face of protests and objections which have been raised. They have decided to agree and now the province of Quebec is the only province which has not agreed. Why? Because the French Canadian ministers and certain French representatives on the other side of the house want to carve out constituencies and change the boundaries of counties in which they were elected in 1930 by very substantial majorities. Why should we not all 53719-337
be men enough to stop these petty criticisms? It is all very well to say that we have had our way for forty years, but that did not prevent hon. gentlemen opposite from being elected. The supposed gerrymandering which took place at the last redistribution did not prevent the Minister of Marine being elected in Chambly-Vercheres. It did not prevent the Postmaster General and other Frencn members now sitting on the other side being elected. This supposed gerrymander could not have been so bad because they were elected in spite of it.
Let them have the courage to go back before the electors who sent them here and whose mandate they have exercised in this house. Let them take a lesson from the man they call their god, from their leader the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and not go to him as they are at the present time with a stuttering and shivering prayer asking that they be taken out of the constituencies which have elected them and be given safer seats made by the carving up of other constituencies. I have never been so seriously convinced as I am at the present time that the answer of the Prime Minister will be: Young men, take courage, because fear has never spelled victory for any man or any party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have listened very patiently every minute of every hour of yesterday and all of to-day to the arguments that have been made >in this house against the bill which is now before this committee for consideration. I have endeavoured to approach the problems dispassionately, but there are certain facts that cannot be overlooked and one would be indeed an unfair and unjust man who would not recognize them. Redistribution in its very nature is a task that has always invoked passions in the House of Commons, sometimes in a moderate and sometimes in a most immoderate way; sometimes because there has been a frank recognition on the part of all parties that an effort is being made to take advantage of redistribution for political purposes; at other times for other reasons.
Let me remind the committee that in the days of the first prime minister of this country there were great difficulties about redistribution and that the leader of the opposition who finally succeeded in destroying the Conservative party in 1896, pledged his party that if he came into power, an effort would be made to have a redistribution effected by a committee of the house. As a matter of fact, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
responsible for one redistribution and one only, in 1903. The census was taken in 1901 and the redistribution was made in 1903. Being curious to ascertain whether there was that measure of perfection that we might expect because a parliamentary committee had been set up, I took the trouble to turn up the journals of the house and it is amazing to find just what those journals disclose. At page 87 of the journals for 1903, there is the following entry:
Ordered, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier have leave to bring in a bill to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
He accordingly presented the said bill to the house, and the same was received and read the first time; and ordered to be read a second time to-morrow.
On a further page there is the entry of the second reading of the bill and the setting up of a committee which was established for the purpose of determining what the boundaries should be. That, I am sure, was regarded as a reasonably fair committee. It consisted of Messieurs Fitzpatrick, Sutherland (Oxford), Hyman, Davis, Borden (Halifax), Haggart and Monk, with instructions to prepare schedules. But before the committee was set up and second reading was given to the bill, a debate arose as to the interpretation to be placed upon the British North America Act and a division occurred, the question being whether there should be referred to the courts the issue as to the legal interpretation to be placed upon the aot. That the government defeated by 72 votes to 37.
The committee did its work and if those who may be interested will take the trouble to turn to page 575 of the journals of that year, they will find that not only were there profound differences in the house, but they were expressed in terms of motions on the third reading in which motions the principles declared for by Mr. Borden in the committee- and the details will be found at page 576- were voted upon in the house again on third reading, the vote being 28 to 65. The principles that Mr. Borden in the committee asked to have passed, one might well have thought, after listening to what has been said here by the opposition, during the last two days, had been declared by them. I mention that because it must be apparent to every thoughtful man in the house that those out of power always charge those in power with failing to apply what they conceive to be the correct principles for redistribution; and those in power declare that they are applying the principles which their opponents applied when they were in power. That is the situa-
tion. There were five or six divisions on the third reading, but I will read only two or three. The first resolution, as it appears on page 575 of the issue of the journals for September 25, 1903, was moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and seconded by Sir William Mulock, that the bill be now read the third time. Mr. Haggart moved, in amendment, seconded by Mr. Kaulbach, that it be recommitted to the whole house for the purpose of rearranging the schedules in accordance with the principles laid down by Mr. Borden to the select committee. Those principles are:
(a)	The municipal county boundaries shall
be those as set forth in chapter 3, revised statutes of Ontario, 1897, and the word "county'' herein shall include any provisional county or territorial district established by the said act.	_
(b)	The separate representation to be allotted to the city of Toronto shall first be fixed and determined before proceeding with the representation of the rural constituencies.
(c)	The unit of representation for such rural and city constituencies shall be determined by deducting from the total population of Ontario the population of the city of Toronto and by dividing the remainder by the total number of seats to be allotted to such rural and city constituencies.
(d)	The population of any city receiving separate representation shall be excluded in computing the population of the county within which it is situate.
(e)	The redistribution of the representation of Ontario shall then be determined as follows:
Then they follow setting forth what counties should be entitled to one member, two members and three members, the maximum rising to 82,000 and making the sum total, after the application of those principles, of 86 members for the entire province.
Then came the question of Prince Edward Island, with a motion and an amendment as to that; then an amendment with respect to Manitoba where the whole schedule was to be dealt with. Finally, on those divisions the redistribution bill was passed. That is the only redistribution bill with which the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier had to deal.
In 1914 the government of Sir Robert Borden had to deal with redistribution. There was set up a select committee which consisted of a larger number of members having regard to the increased size of the house. A debate took place on the second reading and finally a committee was set up consisting of Messieurs Beland, Bennett (Calgary), Buchanan, Macdonald, Pardee, Pelletier, Reid (Grenville), Rhodes and Rogers. Three of the members of that committee are still in the house, and at least one, if not two, of them are members of the other chamber. That was on Febru-

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
ary 9, 1914. As the hon. member for Richelieu has just said, that committee took a long time over its deliberations. Finally it made a report which is found at page 673 of the journals for that year. It will be observed that that committee did not arrive at unanimity, but it made a report, the second part of which reads:
Your committee have prepared and unanimously agreed to report upon the description and the return of members contained in the several electoral divisions, which are set forth in the schedules hereto appended, in respect to the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon territory, and upon the description and the return of the several electoral divisions which are set forth in the schedule hereto appended, in respect to the province of Nova Scotia, with the exception of that portion of the last named schedule which relates to the return of two members for the proposed united counties of South Cape Breton and Richmond, in the province of Nova Scotia, to which a majority of your committee have agreed.
Then followed provisions with respect to Prince Edward Island which had the result, in the end, of an amendment to the British North America Act whereby it was provided the total representation in the House of Commons of any province should not fall below its representation in the Senate. The bill passed, as I say, without amendment. A short time was taken to consider it, some slight amendments were made, and at page 726, on June 12, it wras ordered that the bill be read a third time. It was read a third time, without amendment.
Then came the redistribution of 1924. That there were serious differences in 1924 need not be questioned. That in the end they arrived at what might be regarded as a half compromise is quite apparent, because the bill having been introduced on March 3, 1924, it was given its second reading and referred to a second committee on March 25. I am leaving out the fact that in 1923 the then government endeavoured to pass a redistribution bill. A committee was set up and failed to arrive at a conclusion. In the last minutes of the session the bill was abandoned and set over until 1924.
In 1924 the special committee was set up, and made its first report. The chairman of the committee was the Hon. E. M. Macdonald, Piotou county. Later they prepared a report which is found in the journals of the house of July 11, 1924, at page 546. I direct attention to the fact that the suggestion has been made that this legislation is being pressed in the closing days of the session. As a matter 53719-337i
of fact in 1924 it was dealt with on the last two days of the session, and part of the third; that was all. I mention that only in passing, because I suggest it is not proper to charge that because we are dealing with the bill in the closing days of the session it is part of a deliberate plan. However, about that I shall say something later. The committee will pardon me if I direct attention to the words of the report.
Mr. Macdonald (Pictou), from the special committee to whom was referred Bill 2, an act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, with instructions to prepare schedules to contain and describe the several electoral divisions entitled to return members to this house and to report the same, prescribed the second report of the said committee which is as follows:
Your committee have prepared and unanimously agreed upon the description and the return of members contained in the several electoral divisions, which are set forth in the schedules hereto appended, in respect to the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon territory, and upon the description and the return of members contained in the several electoral divisions which are set forth in the schedules hereto appended, in respect to the province of Ontario, with the exception of the electoral divisions of South Hastings, West Peterborough, Hastings-Peterborough, and Fort William in the said province to which a majority of your committee have agreed.
Your committee have also considered section 4 of the said bill and have unanimously agreed to recommend that the said section be amended. The proposed amendment is appended to this report. and submitted with the several schedules for the consideration of the house.
Some slight changes were made in the Senate with respect to the language of the bill. The words " Missisquoi-Brome " were deleted and for them were substituted the words "Brome-Missisquoi," that being strongly but unsuccessfully advocated in this chamber by Mr. MicMaster.
Let us pause for a moment, endeavouring if possible to be perfectly fair in this matter, and look at the position of the parties in this house, bearing in mind the conditions which existed in the province of Quebec. Let us for a moment look at what the position was in 1921. There were elected to this house from the province of Quebec sixty-five Liberals -see page 316 of the Parliamentary Guide- Conservatives none. So it would appear that when the redistribution was made the Conservative party was without representation in this chamber from the province of Quebec. Behold the result. In the succeeding election, notwithstanding the fact that the Conservative party polled between forty per cent ana

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
forty-five per cent of the entire votes, they did n'ot elect any candidates. I ask this committee if that, in itself, does not give cause for thought. I am endeavouring to be as fair as a man can who has had some little legal training, and I shall stick to a recital of the facts. Will any judge say that the fact I have recited would not, in itself, give cause for thought? Does it not cause every thoughtful man in this house just to ponder a moment on the situation?
Then in 1931 we have another census, and in 1933 we set up a committee. It was a committee which, I submit, must be regarded as a fair and reasonable committee of this house. It was selected after a great deal of care and attention had been given to the matter. From British Columbia there were Mr. Barber and Mr. Reid-I believe I am departing from the strict rules of the house by mentioning names. From Alberta there was a parliamentarian of long experience, the Hon. Charles Stewart, together with Doctor Stanley of Calgary and Mr. Kennedy of Peace River. From Saskatchewan there were Mr. Turnbull and Mr. Totzke; from Manitoba there were Mr. Burns, Mr. Beau-bien and Mr. Heaps. From Ontario, there was, Hon. H. A. Stewart, who became chairman of the committee; Hon. Mr. Manion, succeeded by Doctor Cotnam; Mr. Mac-Nicol and Hon. Mr. Elliott, a former minister of the crown; from Quebec there were Mr. Dorion, Mr. Gobeil and Mr. Mercier of Laurier-Outremont. From New Brunswick there was Mr. Bell; from Nova Scotia, Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Smith of Cumberland. As there was no change possible in Prince Edward Island no member from that province was placed on the committee.
I ask members of this committee if those members were not representative of the different parts of Canada. Is that not reasonable representation? Is that not a reasonable cross-section of this house, for the purpose of arriving at a conclusion? On November 25, this committee was appointed. I made it my business-myself-to have sent to each member of the committee information which had been prepared in the bureau of statistics for the purpose of enabling the committee during the recess to obtain a reasonably fair appreciation of the problems with which they had to deal.
At the threshold of inquiry you have to determine the unit of representation upon which redistribution shall be made. If hon. members who are interested would turn to page 3 of the information prepared by the

bureau of statistics they would find these words:
Unit of representation: While the number of the members of the House of Commons has been growing steadily since confederation, the unit of representation-one-sixty-fifth of the population of Quebec within its boundaries prior to the 1912 extension

has also been increased after each census in consequence of the expanding population of Quebec. The units of representation as shown by the seven decennial censuses taken since confederation, are as follows:	1871, 18,331 persons; 1881, 20,908;
1891, 22,901; 1901, 25,368; 1911, 30,819; 1921, 36,283; 1931, 44,186.
Thus you have in the province of Quebec a more difficult task than you would have ordinarily in other provinces because of its unit of representation being 44,186 and there being 65 members-no increase and no decrease-you have a complex problem; as the former Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) very properly said to-day, a very much more complex problem to deal with than otherwise would be the case.
But the problem has become complicated in two of the largest older provinces by reason of another circumstance, namely the steady trend of population from rural to urban centres. That fact you will find dealt with on page 6 of the information sent out to the members. I will only point out that the entire rural population of the Dominion of Canada in 1931 was 4,804,728 and the urban population 5,572,058; in other words the percentage of rural population in 1931 was 46-30 and urban population 53.70, a change since 1921 from 50-48 rural and 49-52 urban. Now bearing in mind the increased urban population I ask the committee to be good enough to look with me for a moment at just what the situation was with respect to that great centre of population, the island of Montreal. The entire population of Quebec in 1931 was 2,874,255, and of that number 1,060,649 was rural and 1,813,606 was urban. Now let us turn for a moment to the island of Montreal. If the committee will be good enough to turn to page 26 it will be found that the island of Montreal had a population of 1,003,868 souls. I wonder if it has ever occurred to the members of this committee that that is within 57,000 of the entire rural population of the province of Quebec. Imagine the difficulties that confronted the committee-sixty-five seats in the province of Quebec, 1,004,000 people, in round numbers, on the island of Montreal, and 1,060,000, in round numbers, of rural population in the entire province. The committee, confronted with that difficulty, together with a unit of representation of 44,000, realized of course

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
that what could be said with respect to Montreal could be said-with less force, it is true-with respect to Toronto and the rural portions of the province of Ontario.
The committee endeavoured to deal with that problem. Every word that was said yesterday by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott), the former Minister of Public Works, represented the appeal that was made from time to time to that committee not to overlook the rural population. The hon. member for West Middlesex pleaded that there should be no dealing with this matter on a hard and fast mathematical and mechanical rule whereby the representation of the rural population would be so sadly cut down. What was said this morning by the former Minister of Marine, reechoing in part what was said by the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), indicates that if a hard and fast mechanical rule, a purely mathematical rule, is applied, not only will there be departure from county boundaries and municipal and parish lines, but such confusion will be caused by the carving out of constituencies in conformity with mathematical requirements as to bring about a condition which will be at least offensive to the people of the province of Quebec. Yesterday we were reminded that there were large differences in population in some of the counties in Ontario; that one county had 83,000 and another 26,000, one 30.000, another 55,000 and another 75,000. Everything said by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) was said before the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power. The very same considerations w'ere urged. But once in power there has not yet arisen in this country any committee prepared to disregard county boundaries and municipal lines in the provinces. The very plea made in this house by hon. members from Quebec, the very plea made by the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this morning, pointing out. how people become attached to their county, become attached to their county town, become attached to their market town as part of their constituency- everyone knows that is so. Yet I believe that what the former Minister of Marine said is true; after listening to everything that has been said, after looking at the figures as carefully as one can, I am convinced that the time must come when parliament must be prepared to apply a different rule with respect to some of these smaller seats in all parts of Canada than has been heretofore applied. The ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce was perfectly fair when he said yesterday that
the blame does not attach to the committee. He said it attaches to all members of the house, because every representation made to the members, the friendly members of the committee, by the members of this chamber constituted an effort to maintain the status quo. There is no doubt about that. I was struck by the force of what the former Minister of Trade and Commerce said in that regard, because it represented the conviction I had arrived at-and I am going to explain in a moment what my position has been with respect to this redistribution measure. Having seen a committee set up, a committee in which I had confidence, I believed it was not my duty to say to the chairman or any members of it that you should do thus or so with respect to particular areas. I could not tell you to-day definitely what are the boundaries of my own constituency of West Calgary. Doctor Stanley spoke to me from time to time, and I said: Whatever conclusion you arrive at is entirely satisfactory to me. And that represents my position now.
Confronting that problem I put this to my hon. friends opposite; I say to you: Gentlemen, for forty years or more you have been responsible for the boundaries of counties in the provincial legislature and for the distribution as it now stands. There is only one thing I should like to say with regard to the admirable observations made by the former Minister of Marine in some parts of his speech, and that is this, that he cannot have read very carefully this book or he would have observed that the county lines have been departed from in the existing distribution. For instance, Dorchester comprises parts of three counties as the counties are defined by the provincial legislature, and if you will take the list and look at the second word, that is the county name, and the population of the county, you will find that the variation between the county population and the electoral division population represents the extent to which county boundaries have not been followed in Quebec. What is true in Quebec is true in other parts of Canada also.
