I do not allege for a moment, and I do not think it necessary to do so, that in 1924 or in 1903 men so lost their sense of fairness as to desire to do what was unjust and unreasonable to their fellow members. I do not charge that at all, but knowing human nature as I do and knowing the instincts that govern men with respect to political matters I do say that I am perfectly clear that when there was a favour possible by doing a thing in

Redistribution-.1/r. Bennett
one of two ways, with either way just and proper, they would choose that method which gave the greatest benefit to themselves and their friends. Is there any doubt about that? What have we here to-day? The closing appeal of the former Minister of Marine is one which cannot be lightly disregarded in this chamber, but what have we listened to for a day? We have had statements that something was done this way instead of that way; that is what it gets down to, that instead of doing it the way you want it done we have done it the way we want it done. Had there been any voice to raise in this house in 1924-unfortunately there was not-exactly the same thing would have been said. I do say to this committee, sir, that on Saturday last I asked to see the old and new maps of the province of Quebec. Having heard all that I had heard in this house, with the charges that had been made, as man to man I can say frankly that I was amazed when I saw the map that had been prepared. I found that the map of 1924 contained all these jogs, these little differences and variations in order to effectuate what was regarded as a fair redistribution. Then when I took the map of 1933 and looked at the boundaries there shown I saw exactly the same sort of thing, varied, it is true, to meet the changed conditions of population. Undoubtedly where two courses were open our friends chose the course that was more helpful to them.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, just as in 1924 the course chosen was the one more favourable to the party then in power. Now it gets down to a contest as to the acceptance of your plan, under a given contingency, or the plan of the committee under a given contingency; that is the fact. If I may be allowed to say so, when this committee of elder statesmen met, about which I shall have something to say presently, it was amazing how the number of complaints narrowed themselves down to so few, and some of those were capable of simple adjustment. It became apparent, however, that as soon as one point was yielded the whole thing stopped and started all over again. It was just as the former Minister of Trade and Commerce said yesterday; every member was playing his own hand in his desire to secure his own position. As soon as he found that some change had been made to meet a certain condition he thought, "Well, I must have my way too," and the result was that we were getting nowhere.
That was the reason I said to the house the other evening that we had reached agree-
ments with regard to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba. There was very little disagreement with regard to British Columbia; that has been adjusted and the agreement has been signed. The disagreement in Alberta is slight, nothing that I conceive to be very serious, and in the two older provinces and Saskatchewan, to which I shall refer presently, the disagreements were more serious. What do the disputes narrow themselves down to? Simply the complaint that in order to meet a situation that was real-and it has been admitted to be real, for the reasons I have given and for the reasons mentioned by the former Minister of Marine-and in the effort to adjust those actualities of population, of convenience and of the desire, as I have said, to cause as little friction and disturb existing conditions as little as possible, a certain course has been chosen. Some hon. gentlemen say it is highly immoral that these choices should be made in the way they have. The answer given by the committee is this: "We have chosen these because in our opinion these were the most convenient changes to make, and the least inconvenient to all parties concerned." That is the old province of Quebec, and I do not think anyone will say that I have not stated the facts just as they are. I have set them before the committee, not in malice; I have not overstated anything and I am certain that I have not understated the position from the standpoint of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Under those circumstances I wholly agree with what was said by the former Minister of Marine. He made a very earnest appeal for agreement and accommodation but I must remind him that appeals such as his, unless evidenced by conduct, are as faith without works, which is dead. That is the diflficulty. However willing he might be to yield on this or that point the committee finds itself up against an absolute stone wall when it asks that those concessions be made that would at least indicate a reasonable willingness for accommodation. I am not going to traverse all these various constituencies, though I have taken the trouble to go into them with some care. For instance, I find that the basis of population around the city of Quebec now has been equalized within a few hundred, and it is said that this has been done with the least inconvenience to the people affected. It is perfectly clear that the population does not average more than 30,000 per riding in that territory; it is perfectly clear that the unit of representation throughout Canada is 44,000, but I for one believe that in this country at this time it is desirable that we

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
should not treat the rural population on an entirely different 'basis from that which has prevailed hitherto, by making the absolute unit of population 44,000, which would have the effect of cutting down the seats outside the island of Montreal and the cities to a point that in one sense would be almost negligible. In the very nature of things you cannot apply the same tests in the rural portions of the country that you can apply in the cities, and this committee has not endeavoured to do so.
Without going into the details, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I have not yet reached the point where I believe that human nature is so constituted that those who for the moment are out of power are unwilling to recognize that fact. In all sincerity may I say that while the Liberal party is in the ascendancy provincially, and federally in point of the number of members from the province of Quebec, in this parliament there happens to be in power a Conservative administration. Is it not fair to say that hon. gentlemen opposite must recognize that fact, and to recognize the further fact that when a choice has to be made in one of two given ways you must expect that choice to be made in the way that will be most advantageous to the party in power. Is that unfair? Is that not what has always happened in regard to anything? I do appeal to those who sit to the left of the Speaker to recognize that fact with regard to the province of Quebec. I think I understand something of their point of view. I know it is not always easy to reconcile one's self to a fact; it is not always easy to become reconciled to a fact when it is believed that the fact never should have been. But just let me quote one line, if I may, from what Sir William Harcourt said away back in 1882, when Gladstone was moving his measure of closure in the British house:
It is essential to secure to a majority the right to prevail which lies at the bottom of parliamentary institutions. To recognize in one-third or one-quarter of the house an absolute right to postpone indefinitely the_ decision of a question is, in my judgment, to give a formal consecration to the principle of obstruction. Why is it to be assumed that the minority will not abuse their veto when it is taken for granted that the majority will abuse their cloture?
These were the words of Sir William Har-court, who at least was the spokesman for a great school of thought of which Gladstone was the chief, when he was introducing his measure of closure.
I have endeavoured to approach this question not from a partisan point of view, and I suggest to those members of this committee who, representing the majority of deputies
from the province of Quebec, represent also the opposition, or the party that sits to the left of the Speaker in this chamber, that any little inconsistencies or incongruities, or anomalies that appear in the bill can easily be ironed out without any difficulty in the world I was struck this morning with the observations made by the former Minister of Justice. He denounced in unmeasured terms what he conceived to be, as he said, a gerrymander; yet the very illustrations he gave were illustrations which in my judgment proved that a continuance of the condition that now exists would be the perpetuation of an unfair distribution of seats, having regard to population and what followed from the redistribution of 1024. That is all I have to say at the moment with respect to the province of Quebec except to say that, so far as the island of Montreal is concerned, we are faced with a difficulty of the first magnitude. The entire population of that island, I repeat, is equal to the rural population of the province of Quebec less 57,000; and if you accorded to them representation by population they would be entitled to one-tenth practically of the entire representation in this house, which would be 24 seats. The committee have said that 16 seats amply represent what is fair and just with respect to the island of Montreal, and that leaves 49 seats to be distributed between the rural and urban population in the rest of the province of Quebec. Now, the committee have earnestly striven, as everyone can see, not unnecessarily to eliminate seats at this time, not unnecessarily to disturb existing conditions in the rural communities-because the population in many of these counties fell below 30,000, and in some instances below 25,000-but to maintain them, some of them being, I repeat, as strongly Liberal seats as one could possibly find. The committee endeavoured to retain them, having striven to assert this principle, that you could not apply the unit system of 44,000 mathematically to the rural population of that province.
I turn now for a moment to the province of Ontario. There you have the great city of Toronto with its surrounding territory. The population is something less than a million souls. They have necessarily increased the population of that section of Ontario, and you have the same problem which you had in the province of Quebec. The question is: Shall you, as the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested, just simply say, ' There is the unit of population of 44,000; let us go out and ruthlessly apply that mathematically to the whole province of Ontario."

I did not say that.
Redistribution-Mr. Bennett

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was the sense of it.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It meant nothing else.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will read his words-
I have; I have read them to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -he will find that he put forward the idea that population must be the governing factor.
I mentioned two exceptions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What are they?
_ Mr. MALCOLM: I know the Prime Minister does not want to be unfair. I mentioned especially the fact that the small percentage of voters in a city did not justify the unit of population being the same-the small percentage of people polling their votes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, then, made the distinction that in the city, where apparently they thought it unnecessary to go to the polls-
They apparently did not go to the polls.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, the answer to that is that, in the illustrations which the hon. gentleman gave, the people were so certain of the result that they did not think it necessary to go to the polls.
That may be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That seemed to be the case which the hon. gentleman selected for the purpose of illustration. I will not discuss this afternoon the question of compulsory voting, that will have to be done some other tame. I do say however that if you applied the rule of dividing the population of the province of Ontario, outside the great cities, by 44,000 and saying, "There are your seats," you would create complete chaos and dissatisfaction throughout that province, because in that province you have the same situation that exists in the province of Quebec.
The committee have certainly not been governed by political considerations in Ontario. I know exactly what the hon. member for North Bruce contends. I know-at least I have been told, because it is only hearsay and one cannot say one knows-of the difficulties in connection with Southeast Grey and the taking of certain portions of a constituency and putting them in that rather than another. All these are matters of detail, but the great principle is that in the rural part of Ontario there 
has been no application of the rule I have referred to, namely, the division of the population by 44,000. Not only has there been no effort to do that, but because it has not been done you have in Welland to-day 83,000 people represented by one member, just as they were at confederation in that constituency. That cannot be said to be fair; and yet, if you endeavoured to apply the 44,000 rule and set about doing so, you would so disorganize the whole rural population of Ontario as to create a condition not only of dissatisfaction but of chaos. I would point out that the very principles which in 1903 were moved for on the third reading of the redistribution bill-the first redistribution bill of the Liberal party- were principles such as are now asserted by the opposition here. But when the government of Sir Robert Borden were charged with the responsibility of redistribution they realized that you could not apply these principles, and the committee unanimously arrived at this conclusion: You had here a small constituency and there a large one; you had county boundaries, municipal lines, the convenience of a great population, and in some instances the historic and traditional circumstances connected with the riding itself. This committee have not departed from that; if they did, it would be such a radical and complete change applied to the dominion that I do not believe that this house would adopt any such redistribution measure. I do not believe that any government which this country has ever seen could put through a redistribution measure on that basis.
Now, .the eastern provinces are disposed of. Let me say in passing what I said the other day with respect to Nova Scotia. There is the oldest province in which elections have been held in Canada. W'hen Cornwallis signed the warrant for an election in the ward-room of his ship, the first divisions of constituencies were made in Canada. There are a number of counties established in Nova Scotia, counties that have grown up with our municipal system during the course of a century and more. W'hat have you? You have down by the sea Guysborough and Antigonish united, with a population of 25,000. Following along the seaboard you have the old county of Halifax, and you come to Shelburne and Yarmouth; you have Lunenburg and Queens-counties on the Atlantic seaboard. Now, what had the committee to face in that province? There had to be faced the question whether or not jou would break up, as -might have -been done, the county of Colchester, represented in this house by a Liberal. Add half of it to Cumberland and you would still be under your population.

Redistribution-Mr. Bennett
You would not be over the population according to the unit and you have eliminated the one seat that had to be eliminated on the mainland. What did the committee do? Because county lines are so highly regarded in that province it left Cumberland, Colchester and Digby; it left Antigonish-Guysborough with its 25,000 -and left Shelbume-Yarmouth with the addition of the parish of Clare from the county of Digby. It then took the county of Digby, the county of Annapolis and the county of Kings and made them into one riding without disturbing the lines, and this new riding has a population of 50,000. It is said that according to the principles laid down, that is unfair but the committee felt that rather than dismember counties, rather than split them in two and put part of the population here and part there, it was better to have a county which was 6,000 over the unit than to have all the consequent confusion and ill feeling which would arise from following the course I have mentioned. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Short) objected, and very properly so. He still objects and doubtless will voice his resentment when the schedule for Nova Scotia is reached. He says that at his time of life he cannot contest a constituency 125 miles long. I heard some hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan say something about there being 125 miles in a constituency. In the first election to this House of Commons which I contested I was the candidate for the whole district of Alberta. This comprised all the territory from the extreme north, south to the boundary line including Lethbridge, Macleod, Calgary, Edmonton and Wetaskiwin. That was the position in 1900. Mention is made of 125 miles, but I had 300 or 400 miles to cover. In this instance, 125 miles in the province of Nova Scotia means a great deal.
In New Brunswick one member has been dropped from Saint John-Albert, and that is the end of that. There is a Conservative seat again, but other arrangements could have been made in that province.
Prince Edward Island has not been disturbed because it still has four seats.
I have dealt with Quebec; I have dealt with Ontario and I come now to Manitoba. Is it not amazing that in Manitoba where you have such sharp political differences they have been able to arrive at agreement? Each side made concessions and the Liberal party did not go unrepresented. But it realized what the situation was and that arrangement was made.
We come now to the province of Saskatchewan. It was most unfortunate in my judgment that the difficulties in Saskatchewan should have been discussed at such length. What do these difficulties amount to? This one group who say that they constitute the majority in Saskatchewan insist that the redistribution should be made north and south. They say that is the way in which it should be done. There was some little difficulty south of Qu'Appelle and the Saskatchewan river but the committee arrived at some sort of, we will say tentative understanding. We then get into the north country. The province of Saskatchewan under Liberal guidance united the Battlefords and the Battle-fords are now one provincial riding. Is there anything that has been held up to us in days gone by as being more desirable than that wherever possible the federal and provincial boundaries should coincide? That being so, why should there be any great complaint if the committee arrived at that conclusion?
The right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is a former minister of the crown and former prime minister whose constituency Is in Saskatchewan. The former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is the second ex-minister from that province. The former Minister of Agriculture contended that he had been very unjustly and unfairly dealt with. In the end- I desire to remove any misapprehension on the point-the committee agreed to give him the boundaries of the constituency for which he asked. It was not done at my instance and I did not know of its being done until after it was done. As a matter of fact I believed, and I stated my belief, that the extent to which they would go in agreeing to his contention would jeopardize any chance of unity in the whole. And I was right. Look at what we have. Because the committee yielded to the importunities of the former Minister of Agriculture we are now told that the whole thing is bad and wrong and must be set at naught.
That is not all. I was rather surprised when the right hon. leader of the opposition suggested that there was a deep laid plot to have him driven from public life. If I had my choice there is no man I would rather keep in public life than the right hon. gentleman. That is all I have to say. It would be far from me to suggest and I say sincerely that I do not believe that any member of the committee desired that the right hon. gentleman should be driven out of public life by any redistribution made in Prince Albert. AVhat, are the facts? The facts are that the Liberal member from Saskatchewan agreed to
Redistribution-Mr. Bennett

the boundary of Prince Albert being extended south beyond its present boundary. He has said in the committee that he agreed to that, and he has repeated it. It therefore follows that there was recognition by the Liberal member from Saskatchewan that the existing boundaries were wrong. Having recognized that the existing boundaries were wrong, the question then arose as to the extent to which they should be remedied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not been following me carefully. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke), who was the representative of the Liberal party from the province of Saskatchewan on that committee, has admitted that the boundaries of Prince Albert should be rectified. He has admitted that the southern boundary should be extended further south, and he made his extension. The Conservative member from Saskatchewan said that that was not far enough south having regard to the movement of population to the north. There was an acute difference of opinion as to where the boundary should be, whether it should be x miles north or y miles north. That as the only issue. Now, is there not the greatest likelihood for a difference on that point?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not the only issue.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the only issue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend has left out the fact that a considerable part of another constituency has been added to Prince Albert notwithstanding the complaint that Prince Albert was too large and must be cut down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not overlooking that factor. Rectification of the boundary was asked for and there was a difference of opinion as to how it should be effected. That is something that arises in every redistribution or in every case that ever comes up in a court of law. What is the basis of all our institutions? Our whole legal institution is based upon the fact that when there are differences they must be settled, not by fighting as they used to be in the old days but by recourse to the courts. The right hon. gentleman has said very properly that this is the high court of parlia-
ment. It is very seldom that it divides on other than party lines, nevertheless it is the high court of parliament. The issue in Prince Albert is this: How shall the boundaries be rectified, it being admitted that they are wrong at the present time? Let that never be forgotten. How can you talk about indignity or a lack of chivalry being shown on the part of any party or men who say that there is the necessity for this rectification, and admit the only question at issue is: How shall the wrong be righted? That is the issue. Speaking for myself and for the government as well, I say, the government say and every member of the government says that we desire to work no wrong to any man with respect to redistribution, and if on the subject matter under discussion it becomes apparent that the boundaries suggested by the Conservative members of the committee can be adjusted on a fairer or more proper basis, that will be done. But it is wrong to say, when you have an admission of the fact that the boundaries are wrong and the only issue is that of rectification, that therefore your opponents are guilty of all the crimes and *misdemeanours that can be found in the calendar. 1 hat does not make for securing what is desired to be secured; it does not make now and it never has made. I leave it to the judgment of this committee, if every member of it ever heard a more provocative speech than that which the leader of the opposition made yesterday morning. But it was not and it will not be met in that spirit, so far as we are concerned. I repeat that in respect to the province of Saskatchewan it has been in the main admitted that there must be rectifications; that is admitted by everybody. Why? Because the population has moved north. One hon. gentleman says that that will rectify itself in time by the population moving back. He may be right, but in the meantime we lnave to deal with actualities and realities, and the reality is that there is no change in the number oi members to be returned and that therefore all one has to do is to adjust the same membership to new boundaries for a shifted population; that is all.
The facts disclosed before this committee indicate that the matter has been approached, if the individuals were left alone, in a spirit of compromise and accommodation; but some people say: No,, we will not do this; that is all there is about the matter; we are not going to do it. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. MoPhee) said that he did not like the name "Touchwood." Touchwood is a name

Redistribution-Mr. PouLiot
older even than the fifty years of Yorkton, but if it will be any satisfaction to change the name from Touchwood to Yorkton, it will be changed. One is not to have a quarrel over redistribution merely because a man prefers Yorkton to Touchwood. Some hon. members suggest that the word "Battle-ford" should be "Battlefords." The fact is that the original manuscript contained the word "Battlefords," and it will be so if that will appease the feelings of the hon. gentlemen in the matter. But if you go through the whole representation of Saskatchewan, you have just this difference: an unwillingness on the part of those who sit to the left of the Speaker to recognize that if the choice has to be made between a line that way and a line this way to accomplish the same result, the choice lies with their opponents, they being a majority in the house, and not with them. Should not that fact be recognized? Is that unfair? That is all that is at issue.
I am not yet advised as to the whole issue in Alberta and not having had an opportunity to discuss it fully with anyone who could inform me, I am not going to do more than say that I believe the former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) with his conciliatory spirit, and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) will have no difficulty in working out that problem. But let me say this: Alberta is a difficult province to redistribute. Why? On account of the mountains and rivers, and in building of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the crossing of the Battle river was one of the great difficulties experienced by the engineers. You have the Saskatchewan river, the Battle river, the Bow river. When we were dealing with redistribution as long ago as 1914, the difficult problem was what to do with that centre seat that became Bow River. It represented just what was left of the rest of the prov-vince; that was the only way in which it could be worked out and there was great difficulty in doing so. To the west you have that long range of mountains; away up in the northern part of the province you had the hon. member for Peace River representing half an empire and a new seat had to be found there. It has been given the name of Jasper-Edson. There had to be retained by readjustments the seats in the south and one more seat added to the north. In the readjustment, having regard to population, I daresay there may be some difficulties; there were in 1914. I remember in the case of the late Doctor Clark who represented the constituency of Red Deer, the line as drawn and as it remained for weeks put the late Doctor Clark
and myself in the west riding of Calgary. The problem which engaged the attention of the committee then was whether the line should be drawn so many townships south or so many further north. To-day the problem of the boundaries of Bow River is one of some difficulty, but I think there should be no really insurmountable obstacle in the way of its solution.
As regards British Columbia, since this discussion began an agreement has been made that, I trust, is satisfactory to everybody, as I believe it is. On the mainland there was a certain area that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) thought should properly go to Vancouver North, and to Vancouver North it has gone. That has been arranged. It is only a small matter, and on a question of choice it may be the majority of the committee prefer it should go some other place, to Comox-Alberni, but the wishes of both Mr. Munn and Mr. Neill, if I might mention their names, have been met, and that part of the mainland, at least that portion from Bute inlet south, now comprises the constituency of Vancouver North.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons-Right Hon. R. B. Bennett-Mr. Stirling in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have to attend at another place, so I shall continue my remarks at another time.
Is clause 1 carried?

No. Some newspapers have stated that in opposing the schedule and sections of this bill, members are struggling for their political lives. I am not afraid of my political future. For over eight years I have represented my constituency and have done the best I could for my people. I have abandoned a profitable legal practice to give all my time to my parliamentary duties. My electors appreciate that
Redistribution-Mr. Poidiot

fact, and I am very thankful to them for what they have done for me.
Every member of parliament incurs a great number of responsibilities, and in staying here during long sessions, and in abandoning his private business he sacrifices a great deal. For instance, early last year I was busily engaged in some personal work which I have not yet completed. I resumed my work here in Ottawa, intending to use the library, and was told that I could not have the services of a stenographer and could not even have a typewriter if I did not fulfil entirely my parliamentary duties. I did1 so conscientiously and to the best of my ability, and I am very much surprised to hear some hon. members opposite complain that I take too much of the time of the house. Perhaps some of them work as much as I do; I do not boast of working twenty hours a day. I do say however that none of them works harder. When I come here Saturday afternoons and Sundays to work in my little office upstairs, when I receive books from the library I see hon. members in the building, but I very seldom see any who come as regularly as I do. I do not say that by way of boasting, but merely to place some facts before the committee. I see the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and I see the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) who stays here some week ends. I see other hon. members from the west. At times I meet my genial^ friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) who comes here on Sundays. We are all doing our best, and any hon. member will say that we cannot do that without a great amount of sacrifice.
My second statement is that I ask nothing from the government. I ask for nothing. I ask for no favours. I wish only to put the facts before the house in the same manner as I would put the evidence of a witness before a judge who in the first instance states such evidence is not necessary but admits it might be useful at the court of king's bench. When I speak I am not speaking particularly to the government; they may take it if they wish. I am very independent about it. I place myself on record to show what I have said, and that the proof or the evidence is complete. When I go back to my people I will tell them that I have put those facts before the Prime Minister and his colleagues, and if they do not listen to the remarks I make in plain English, they will be judged accordingly.
My only reason for t>eing here to-night, when I should have been attending the funeral of a dear friend in my constituency, is that I feel it my duty to support petitions which

have .been sent in regular and due form by heads of families in my constituency to this House of Commons protesting against the proposed changes. In doing so I am following their example. They have been faithful to me; they have been devoted to me, and I intend to be just as faithful and devoted to them.
I cannot understand how hon. members opposite can say: "Those people at so and so may be excellent people, but we cannot listen to them. The Paquet family is a great family, but we may dispense with them, and it will not matter whether they vote in this or that constituency." When a man has his heart in the right place he cannot forget the ties which bind him to those who for yearn and years have been so kind to him. In my constituency there are about 20,000 voters. In that number there are only about one hundred people who have not voted for me at least at one election. I know them. I do not know if there are many hon. members who can say the same thing. I know by name about ninety-nine per cent of my electors. I know the history of each of them, and last year when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) came to my constituency with the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) there came from distances as far away as sixty or eighty miles about eight hundred people, in spite of the bad weather. I introduced each one to the leader of my party by giving each person's name and family history. I know those people, and it is because I know them that I love them. It is because I love them that I will not let anyone take them away from me, even by brute force.
Another reason for my speaking is that Bill No. 2 to readjust the representation in the House of Commons does not bear the name of any junior member of the cabinet. It bears the name of the Prime Minister himself. It is a measure of such importance that I am in duty bound to put all the facts before the house in order that the Prime Minister and his colleagues may see to it that something is done. But mark you, sir, I ask for nothing, the facts will speak for themselves. I ask for no favours. At the same time I have no fear-I never had any.
Why should you?

The history of the legislation on redistribution as given by the right hon. Prime Minister this afternoon is far from complete. I am here to express the viewpoint not only of the electors of Temiscouata but also of the electors of the province of Quebec.

The Royal Assent
May I take this opportunity to offer my warmest congratulations to my hon. friends who spoke yesterday, and especially to the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) who gave such admirable orations to-day. Sir, let us go back eighty years, to 1853. At that time an enactment was passed creating new electoral constituencies in the province of Quebec. I will speak only of the province of Quebec, because while I do not know the details of what happened in other provinces, I am very familiar with what has been done in the province of Quebec.
In 1853 an enactment was passed setting the boundaries of many constituencies in Quebec which have existed until now. This piece of legislation has served for provincial as well as federal elections-for provincial elections until 18S6 and for federal until 1892. In the province of Quebec in 1886 the only change was to divide three constituencies, that of Chicowtimi-Saguenay, that of Drummond-Arthabaska and that of Richmond and Wolfe, which had been united in 1867, in order to have only 65 seats in the province. The only change made by that legislation in 1886 was to make the constituencies exactly as they were before confederation. In the federal ridings minor changes were made in 1882, minor changes had been made previously in 1872, but until the gerrymander of 1892 the legislative enactment that served for provincial purposes served at the same time for federal purposes.
There is another thing that I wish to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman: always the federal acts relating to redistribution in the province of Quebec have referred to the provincial electoral districts after the new legislation had been passed in the province of Quebec. For instance we see the names of those constituencies which do not exist for federal purposes in their entirety; Papineau, Fron-tenac, Matapedia, Abitibi-Temiscamingue, Charlevoix East, Charlevoix West, Gaspe West and Gaspe East, Papineau, Roberval, Lake St. John East, Lake St. John West. May I now tell the Prime Minister that the provincial boundaries are as much respected in the province of Quebec as they are in Nova Scotia; they are just as sacred in Quebec as in Nova Scotia, and I do not see why what is good for Nova Scotia is not good also for Quebec.
The right hon. gentleman spoke about redistribution that had been made under the first Prime Minister of Canada. If my memory serves me rightly the first Prime Minister of Canada after Confederation was
Sir John A. Macdonald. In 1872 under Sir John A. Macdonald there was a redistribution. What was done by that act, 35 Victoria, chapter 13? St. Felix du Cap Rouge was transferred from Portneuf to Quebec. There were three new electoral districts in the city of Montreal. I mean that the electoral districts already existing in the city of Montreal were changed in 1872. That is all that Sir John A. Macdonald did in the first redistribution after confederation. And mark you, sir, even Portneuf county and Quebec counts'- were not defined in that year by a federal statute, but the description of that constituency in 1872 was found in the old statute of 1853 that I have already referred to.
In 1882, while Sir John A. Macdonald was still alive, by 45 Victoria, chapter 3-and I would ask my hon. friend the Solicitor Genr eral to listen to me; these are things that might interest him, because yesterday hie proved that he did not know even the number of the Quebec seats in the local house.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons-Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.-Mr. Stirling in the chair.

In 1882 the act 45 Victoria chapter 3 was passed. The townships of Sala-

berry, Wolfe and Grandison were transferred from Argenteuil to Terrebonne, and the same year, by the same legislation, St. Monique was transferred from Terrebonne to Two Mountains. In that act there is a new description of the electoral district of Bellechasse: Madeleine islands are annexed to Gaspe and Anticosti island is made part of Chicoutimi-Saguenay. That is all. This means that in the redistribution of 1872 and 1882 only minor changes were made in the legislation of 1853, which served also for provincial purposes. On June 6, 1891, Sir John Macdonald died-the first Prime Minister of Canada since confederation. Sir John Macdonald cannot therefore be held responsible for the gerrymander of 1892. What W'as done in 1872 and 1882 resulted only in slight changes in very few constituencies. In 1892 a real gerrymander was perpetrated by a moribund government. I will not enter into details; I will only quote a few words from my late leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and also a statement made by one of the Conservative ministers of the time, the Hon. Mr. Ouimet. I will give the page of Hansard so that the Minister of Marine may easily find it among the records. On April 29, 1892, Mr. Laurier, as he was then, said, as reported at page 1866:
I must say at once that as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, in so far as I can see it at first sight, the apportionment seems to me to have been the most arbitrary that could have been designed. I am sorry, sir, that those who were in charge of that measure from the province of Quebec did not choose to follow the principle which was laid down as far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned; that is to say, of making the changes in the line of existing divisions.
On the same date Mr. Laurier said:
But when we come to the counties south of the St. Lawrence river in the province of Quebec, where the strength of the Liberal party has always been for twenty years or more, we find gerrymander on such a scale that it will be impossible to recognize the counties now in existence. No attention has been paid to existing limits, parishes which have been united together for very many years are now divided and are jumbled over into five or six different counties. The county of Vercheres, an old county which was represented in the old parliament of Canada by Sir George Cartier, for, I believe, more than 15 years, now disappears and is distributed into three different counties, Richelieu, St. Hyacinthe and Chambly.
I would remark here that history repeats itself.
Then the county of Chambly receives a portion of the county of Rouville, and the county of Rouville receives a portion of St. Hyacinthe. if I remember aright, and a portion of Bagot also. What reason or what

Redistribution-Mr. Pouliot
justification can there be for that? As far as the city of Montreal and the county of Hoehelaga are concerned, I cannot speak with very great accuracy because the limits have been given in only a very imperfect manner, but so far as I can see enough has been given to enable me to congratulate the Minister of Public Works, who had in the county of Laval a very soft bed before, and who will have in the new county of Laval a still softer one now.
What I have just read appears at page 1867 of Hansard of the date mentioned. Now there is not only one minister who is preparing a soft bed for himself; there is the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), there is the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), and there is the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre). They are all looking for Marshall mattresses in the province of Quebec but they will find thorns.
Now let me quote what Mr. Ouimet said. I am sure it will interest every member of the house, because that gentleman used exactly the same language as was used to-day by my hon. friends the Minister of Marine and the Solicitor General. He is reported on page 1870 of Hansard of April 29, 1892, as follows:
... we thought it would be very useful to temper the very pronounced Liberal colour of St. Hyacinthe by adding to St. Hyacinthe the two parishes of St. Mare and St. Antoine.
As to Bagot, we had to take from Richelieu the parish which was next to it and which properly belongs to it, and my hon. friend, the member for Bagot, was so sensitive that he was afraid of being open to the charge of having taken away too many of his opponents in the parishes of St. Pie and St. Dominique, and he took the Liberal parishes from Drummond and Arthabaska, which have already too much population. These two Liberal parishes he expects to manage so that in the future they will be good Conservatives. Those are St. Guillaume and St. Bonaventure.
Is that not the same thing we have heard to-day? The story repeats itself. But what was the flaming language used by Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself, a man who was always very prudent in his expressions? Forty-one years ago, referring to the redistribution drafted by the Conservative party, he said, as reported on page 1862 of Hansard of April 29, 1892, "that is a gerrymander with a vengeance." Referring to this bill as it relates to the province of Quebec, I use the same words as those used by Sir Wilfrid Laurier-this is a gerrymander with a vengeance. That is why we fight it and will fight it to the last.
This morning the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), my leader in the province of Quebec, said some kind things about my constituency and myself. I want to tell him how grateful I am and how much I appreciate his kind words. I appreciate them the more because he was born in my constituency. He knows the different places just as well as I do; he knows the people just as well as I do
and he likes them just as much. The only trouble is that perhaps they like him a little more than they do me.
The intention of the government is to take three parishes away from the east side of Temiscouata constituency, the parishes of St. Jean de Dieu, Ste. Francoise and Trois Pistoles. They are taking away the parish of Notre Dame du Portage on the west side, a very beautiful parish.

He should not laugh when we are talking about these matters. This is not a joke and I am most serious. He should fix his hair with a brush and it would help him. I am sorry I cannot do it for him but I am too far away. The statute contains this description:

I therefore deem it my duty to rise in the house and furnish the committee with certain information which, in addition to those already given, might probably induce this committee on redistribution, to accept our fair and rational requests.
At present, the county of Terrebonne is surrounded by the five following counties: Argenteuil comprising a population of 18,580, with eighteen municipalities and 7,900 voters; Labelle, comprising a population of 30,953; Laval-Two Mountains, with a population of 30,434, 30 municipalities and 13,700 voters; Joliette, with a population of 27,959,	18

I understand, sir, that when the study of the redistribution of the counties in Quebec and throughout the country was first taken up, the question of the required unit of population in each county was broached. Must wo be forced, we representatives of rural counties to acept the principle that the representation of urban centres must be increased to the detriment of that of rural sections? I shall not delay the house in discussing this principle, because we will have to accept it such as it is. The committee has therefore decided to add three constituencies to the city of Montreal and two in the northern parts of Quebec. To reach this aim it was necessary to choose the localities where these constituencies would be created. The committee cast its eyes on the map, north of Montreal, and found that a redistribution could be carried out there and thus solve the problem in a fair and rational way. The following is what was decided. Argenteuil, at present, has a population of 18,000.

Why then remove nearly 9,000 people from the county of Labelle to place -them in -the county of Argenteuil?

The county of Montcalm is annexed to Joliette increasing its population to 41,392, with 35 municipalities. Therefore, this Council strongly protests against all measures or steps taken to carry out this division.
That copy of this resolution be forwarded to Mr. L. E. Parent, member for the county, with a request to strongly support it.

Will one single member of the committee on redistribution still persist in imposing on the hon. representative of Laval-Two Mountains, 6,000 people who, by this resolution passed by the representatives of the municipality, refuse to join the county of Laval-Two Mountains. May I point out that this resolution was adopted. . .

In what year?
[Mr Parent.]

I shall inform the hon. member. It is exactly what I am looking at. It is dated May 2, 1033.
An hon. MEMBER (Trans.): At what hour?

At the regular horn- of the council's meetings. Since that date-Wednesday of last week-municipal elections were held in that locality and all the members of the council were re-elected. This resolution, therefore, expresses the wish of the people. Notwithstanding this fact, an attempt is made to transfer to the county of Laval-Two Mountains, 6,000 people who entirely refuse to form part of any other county than the beautiful county of Terrebonne, of which this parish has formed part since the county was established.
Will the hon. member permit me to ask a question?
Certainly.

Would the scheme proposed by the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin), namely the merging of the county of l'Assomption-Montcalm with the county of Joliette, receive the approval of the hon. member for Terrebonne?

I certainly cannot object, my county is in no way affected; nevertheless, the intention is to deprive me of Ste. Therese and St. Janvier, and I am opposed to that. Will the hon. member allow Ste. Therese to remain in Terrebonne? First of all, is he authorized to give me a definite answer? If it were his neighbour, the hon. member for Quebec Montmorency (Mr. Dorion), chairman of the sub-committee on redistribution for the province of Quebec, I could rely more on such an answer-however, I do not expect an answer from him.
I strongly protest, sir, against the county of Terrebonne being gerrymandered, I resent any single parish being taken away from Terrebonne. And why? Because the county of Terrebonne is not a creation of recent date, in Quebec. It is one of the first counties established before confederation. It was established before 1825. It is an historical county because of the men who represented it. The following is a list of its representatives: In 1841, Terrebonne was represented in Parliament by the Hon. J. E. Turcotte; in 1844, by the Hon. L. H. Lafontaine; in 1848, by the Hon. L. M. Viger; in 1851, by the Hon. A. M. Morin; in 1854, by the Hon. G. M. Prevost; in 1857, by the Hon. L. S. Morin; in 1863, by Mr. Labreche Viger and at Confederation by the Hon. Louis Franqois R. Masson, who became Lieutenant-Governor of the province

Redistribution-Mr. Parent
of Quebec, and who represented Terrebonne until 1878. His successors were: In 1882, the Hon. Guillaume Alphonse Nantel, who later on was Minister of Agriculture in the provincial government; and in 1896, Mr. L. A. Chauvin. Up to 1896, all the representatives of this county formed part of that conservative phalanx of that period. To-day, it is proposed to detach from this county parishes which placed their trust in the Conservative party's predecessors. The Conservatives are acting thus because, since 1896, the county of Terrebonne changed its political allegiance. It was the Hon. Raymond Prefontaine who, in 1900, won this county to the Liberal fold. Since then, it was represented:	In 1908, by Doctor Desjardins; in 1911, by the Hon. Wilfrid Bruno Nantel, who was a member of the government at Ottawa, for a number of years and later, a member of the railway commission. In 1921 this county was represented by the Hon. J. E. Prevost, who to-day is in the Senate.
Have you not forgotten the name of Sir Adolphe Chap-leau? He also represented that county.
He represented it in Quebec.
You forgot to mention him just now.

He represented the county in the Quebec Legislature. You have no knowledge of your parliamentary history. Purchase a dictionary and an encyclopedia, and study them.
The members of the committee, sir, do not. seem to be greatly impressed by the principles laid down by the one whose name is often on their lips, and also by this great French-Canadian statesman who was a credit to our race and country, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to whom we often refer. Members opposite often quote Macdonald and, we also delight in hearing praises bestowed on this great statesman. Sir John A. Macdonald. Do you think, sir, that if the latter was present at this sitting he would advocate the same policy as the one we have just heard uttered by the right hon. Prime Minister?
What was Sir John A. Macdonald's policy? According to Hansard of 1872, p. 929, referring to the policy of preserving the identity of counties, Sir John A. Macdonald expressed himself as follows:
It is, I think, a grand system that the people of Canada should have the opportunity of choosing for political promotion the men in whom they have most confidence and of whose abilities they are fully assured. All that great advantage is lost by cutting off a portion of two several counties and adding them together for
electoral purposes only. Those portions so cut off have no common interest: they do not meet together and they have no common feeling except that once in five years they go to the polls in their township to vote for a man who may be known in one section and nothin another. This tends towards the introduction and development of the American system of caucusses by which wire-pullers take advantage of their political ability only, and not from any personal respect for them.
Then, why did the hon. member change his political allegiance?
I was never a Conservative. I wonder whether you, yourself, changed.

Order,
please!

If the hon. member never changed, it is because his heart is in the wrong place.
Three municipalities, sir, are to be detached from the county of Laval-Two Mountains. The reason, so far as it affects Laval, is to justify the annexation of three municipalities of the county of Terrebonne to that of Two Mountains. I closely followed, this afternoon, the hon. Minister of Marine who stated that-when it was a question affecting Vaudreuil-Soulanges, there could be no discussion about crossing the Ottawa river over two bridges so as to secure a few votes in the county of Jacques Cartier. The hon. minister is quite aware that there are two bridges spanning the river des Prairies and leading to Pont-Viau, l'Abord-a-Plouffe and Laval-des-Rapides, three municipalities situated across the river. Why does he state it is not to the advantage of VaudreuiLSoulanges? It is neither to the advantage of Laval. Why oblige voters to cross a river? I cannot follow his argument; however, I state that the same principle should apply everywhere, an if one is wrong, so is the other.
Hear, hear!

The right
hon. Prime Minister, this afternoon, with all the eloquence we agree he possesses . . .
Hear, hear!

. . . stated in the course of his remarks, that he had recommended to the committee to respect the boundaries of counties as regards Nova Scotia.
Does not this principle apply as well to Quebec? If the boundaries of the counties
Redistribution-Mr. Parent

of Nova Scotia were respected, why were not the demarcation lines of the counties of Terrebonne and Laval-Two Mountains respected? The same principle should apply as much in
one section of the country as in the other.
In his remarks on redistribution the hon. Minister of Public Works stated:
Redistribution should be based on the proportion of population with no greater disturbance than necessary.
Is it not, sir, disturbing a county to detach a section comprising three municipalities? Bear in minid that the parishes of Ste. Therese and St. Janvier are crossed by the national highway from the intersection of the railway at Ste. Therese, as far as St. Jerome, and that the highway which now crosses the county of Terrebonne from its southern portion to its northern extremity will be shortened by 14 miles, just for the pleasure of annexing three municipalities of Laval-Two Mountains. The Ste. Therese railway, the first built in a northern direction, that famous line, the work of one whom many of you know by reputation, the "cure" Labelle. If the latter was in the house this evening, as he so often was in Quebec to defend the rights of the settler and help colonization north of Montreal-he was then known as the "King of the North"- what would he think? He would feel shocked; no words would express his indignation because of the transfer of the parish and town of Ste. Therese from the county of Terrebonne; because of the removal of the only classical institution from the county of Terrebonne. Are such reasons not sufficient to convince the committee that they should reconsider their decision?
The first reason I set forth is that the hon. Postmaster General, who represents the county of Laval-Two Mountains, does not request Ste-Therese or St. Janvier. He perhaps does not state that he objects to them, but he has not made the request. Why hand them over to him if he does not request them? Permit me to keep them, because I want them. They form part of the county, and if they have not been as faithful to our cause as I was entitled to expect, nevertheless I foresee that there will be a change at the next election. At the last Dominion election, the town of Ste-Therese gave the Liberal candidate a majority of 263 votes; while the parish of Ste-Therese unfortunately outnumbered this majority. Why? Because the Conservative party had placed their election agents throughout the rural districts of Quebec. They did not neglect the county of Terrebonne and told our good farmers that they had been [Mr Parent.]
forsaken by the Dominion government so far as the tuberculin test of their cattle was concerned and furthermore that they were not receiving for their butter the price to which they were entitled. They promised them 40 cents per pound for their butter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.
My time has expired. I trust that I have sufficiently pleaded my cause, and that I shall be permitted, in all fairness, to retain Ste-Therese and St. Janvier.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, in
rising to speak I am not so conceited as to think that I shall convince my hon. friends opposite who are on the point of perpetrating the monstrous injustice embodied in this bill, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) recently put it, that the measure must be carried even if to do so, the brutal force of the majority must be resorted to.
I cannot do less,- however, than protest in the strongest way possible, against this shameful injustice of blotting out from -the electoral map of this country the county of L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm, by annexing the county of Montcalm to that of Joliette and the county of L'Assomption to that of Terrebonne. The committee seems to ignore that the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm has a population of 29,188, and that it could have been possible to suppress another county, among the twenty others that have a smaller population.
I wish to make it clear to the house that in the attitude I take I am not prompted by personal gain and I have two excellent reasons for that: first, after devoting almost half of my existence to public life and served to the best of my ability according to my humble gifts, my county and country, I cannot expect that I shall be spared many more years in politics. Another reason, perhaps as important as the first, from a personal viewpoint, is that the annexation, as embodied in the bill, of the county of L'Assomption, where I reside, with the county of Terrebonne, where I practised my profession as notary during the first seven years, cannot but appeal to me on more than one score, because I am certain of finding there a great number of my old friends with whom I fought for the great cause and contributed my quota in electing the hon. Raymond Prefontaine, Jean Prevost and Poetor Desjardins, all three of whom I cherish the memory.

Redistribution-Mr. Seguin
However, above all personal interest, and speaking purely and simply as the faithful servant of those who for a quarter of a century have honoured me with their confidence, I cannot do otherwise than to state in the house and before the country that the injustice that the present leaders of the Conservative party are on the point of perpetrating is most iniquitous and greatly to the detriment of the best interests of these good farmers of L'Assomption-Montcalm, whom I have the privilege of representing in the house.
First, when in 1914, the Conservative government of that date thought proper of merging the counties of L'Assomption and Montcalm, they recognized that this section of Quebec was bound by the same interests and differed from most of all other rural counties of our province, because a special industry, that of tobacco, proper to that district, made of the two counties of L'Assomption-Montcalm a necessary entity.
Later on, always bearing in mind the special industry of this part of Quebec and the particular interests of the .tobacco growers who are so numerous in these two counties, the government, at the cost of many hundred thousands of dollars, established and maintained an experimental farm of tobacco which to-day is the pride and has benefitted the entire farming community of L'Assomption-Montcalm and the neighbourhood.
May I add, sir, that there exists another primordial reason which tends to promote the union of the two counties of L'Assomption and Montcalm, it is the numerous associations existing in this county, such as the Tobacco Growers' Association of L'Assomption-Mont-ca'lm, the Co-operative Tobacco Society of L'Assomption-Montcalm and others.
By its new scheme the Conservative government also disregards the boundaries of the judicial district, detaches .the county of L'Assomption from the Joliette district so as to annex it to the district of Terrebonne and thereby tends to destroy the mode of life, customs, judiciary relations, etc., of the people of L'Assomption to which up to this day the natural course of life has linked them. W hat will be the result of this new scheme? The present population of the county of Joliette is 27,585, that of Montcalm 13,865, which will give the new county of Joliette-Montcalm a population of 41,450.
The population of the county of Terrebonne is 38,611, that is when the 5,651 required by the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) are deducted. I say required by the Postmaster
General, although my hon. friend from Terrebonne (Mr. Parent) just stated that he did not ask for them. One thing certain is that he will not give up this annexation to his county. Therefore, by removing from the county of Terrebonne the 5,651 people of Ste-Therese, town and parish, and St. Janvier, the population of Terrebonne is thereby reduced to 32,960; then, by adding a population of 15,323 from the county of L'Assomption, the new county of L'Assomption-Terrebonne will have a population of 48,283. You will admit, sir, that these figures are rather large, if compared to those of a great number of counties of Quebec but especially to those of the county of Argenteuil, even after being increased.
What are we to think also of the 155 square miles area or more of the new county of L'As-somption-Teirrebonne? It will certainly be an imposing county which, owing to its large population and area, will certainly do honour to the one who will represent it. However, you will agree with me, sir, that this county seems to have too large a population and an area of unreasonable size. Why not allow the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm to remain as it is with its population of 29,188?
I cannot therefore think otherwise that the present bill, so far as the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm is concerned, is most unfair, cannot be justified and will be greatly detrimental to the people of this county as a whole, and more especially to the tobacco growers. The particular interests of the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm require that it be not split up, and as a last resort, I think that, in order not to harm the material interests of L'Assomption-Montcalm, it would be infinitely better for it to be, as a whole, annexed to another electoral division, if hon. members opposite persist in their desire to see it disappear, because it has opposed their policy.
I deemed it my duty to protest against the serious consequences which will have to be borne by the good farming community which I have the honour to represent in the house. In closing my remarks I again strongly protest against the despicable iniquity and incredible injustice which is being perpetrated against the constituency of l'Assomption-Montcalm.

Mr. Chairman, at this late hour, I do not intend to delay at length the house in discussing the present bill. Moreover, the interests of my county, as well as those of Yamaska, were admirably defended this morning and this

Redistribution-Mr. Dubois
afternoon by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin).
I, however, wish to protest on behalf of my constituents against this bill known under various names, which, however, I shall simply designate for the present, as an unfair measure, so as to remain within the bounds of a frank and loyal discussion.
Useless to state that I resent the odium of this redistribution bill, since I protest against this gerrymander which the opposition want to inflict on the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska. You will allow me, sir, to state what took place in committee, since the present bill was introduced. The first scheme, sir, conceived by hon. members opposite was to annex Yamaska to Drummond and Nicolet to Arthabaska; moreover to detach from the county of Nicolet the town of Nicolet, the principal town of the county, the parishes of StenPerpetue and Ste-Brigitte-des-Saults so as to annex them to the county of Yamaska-Drummond. The intention was to also detach from my county the parishes of St-Pierre, Ste-Cecile and Ste-Sophie so as to annex them to the county of Lotbiniere. The scheme was absurd. On May 9, in the presence of Mr. Alfred Gaudet, advocate of Nicolet, my opponent at the 1930 election, and Mr. Comtois, defeated candidate in the county of Yamaska, I met the hon. members in charge of the sub-committee on redistribution. After giving my explanations, the members of the committee decided to reconsider their decision. Finding that the first scheme was absolutely absurd, the committee decided to make the present changes, at the suggestions, probably, of Mr. Comtois.
He is the future candidate.
Instead of adhering to the first scheme, the committee decided to annex Nicolet to Yamaska. I was in fact requested to effect a compromise in the matter.
You were wrong.

It is unfair for the majority to ask for a vote; however, if such be their wish they possess the power to do so. If the majority of the house wishes to complete the shameful deed begun in the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska, it is free to do so. I do not intend to say unpleasant things to my hon. friends opposite. I shall put off doing so until we discuss the bill item by item.

Meanwhile, I intended to discuss matters with our good friends and request them to reconsider their decision and weigh every circumstance and reason which tend to favour the complete merging of the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska and not those that tend against the annexation of parts of these counties. I hope to reach an understanding with our friends. When they hear the reasons I shall set forth and after pondering over those given this morning by the hon. member for Richelieu, I am sure that they will find it only fair, reasonable and right to preserve intact the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska by merging them. I have no objection that Yamaska and Nicolet be merged. Under present circumstances, this merging would be but natural, because the county of Yamaska has not actually a sufficient population to remain on the federal map. Moreover, I have among the people of Yamaska a great number of friends both Conservatives and Liberals. I shall take pride in seeing them form part of the county of Nicolet, and I am willing to welcome them with open arms, because these people have the same habits and characteristics as the people of Nicolet. They belong to the farming classes as do those from Nicolet; they have about the same needs, habits and mentality.
The committee should not detach from the county of Yamaska half of the small parish of St. Michel in order to place it in the county of Richelieu. No doubt that the people of Yamaska would find good friends in the county of my hon. friend from Richelieu, but why split in half this small parish which has formed part of the county ever since confederation. There is no more reason to do this than there is to detach from the county of Nicolet the parishes of St-Pierre, Ste. Cecile, Ste. Sophie, Manseau, Le-mieux and Ste. Marie. These parishes form part of the county of Nicolet ever since Confederation. Why thus split up two counties where people have the same habits, the same mode of life, the same interests; two counties which form part of similar judicial districts and have the same provincial requirements? The county of Nicolet is a distinct entity in provincial matters, as well as the county of Yamaska. Why detach from these counties these six parishes and half of another.
I beg of the committee, of hon. members opposite to be fair in this matter. By treating me fairly, they will, at the same time, show their spirit of justice to the people of these few parishes.
I broke the news of this division to my constituents as well as those of Yamaska, and I
